title: Soil, water and crops: how soil holds water for roots, and why a field of beans feeds the next crop

summary.text: Stand a cup of dry sand and a cup of fine dry soil in a tray of water. In an hour, the water has crept up both cups against gravity, but at very different speeds. Farmers use this every day when they cover soil with straw to keep the water in. They also know a second puzzle. A field tired by rice grows better rice after a crop of moong or groundnut, even though nobody added anything. Your child tests how water climbs in soil, how salt stops seeds, and why bean roots carry tiny helpers who pull nitrogen out of the air.
summary.art: A kitchen counter with three clear cups of sand, gravel and fine soil standing in a shallow tray of blue water, with the water line climbing different heights in each cup, and a bean plant with knobbly roots lying beside them.

intro.hook: Dip the corner of a dry cloth into a bowl of water and leave it. Slowly the water climbs the cloth, up and up, with nobody pushing it. Soil does the same thing. So why does the top of a bare pot dry out in a day, while the soil under a layer of straw stays damp?
intro.text: Water can climb through soil because of the tiny gaps between the grains. How high it climbs depends on how small the grains are. In this unit you measure the climb in gravel, sand and fine soil. You find out what salt does to seeds, and how a cover of leaves saves water. Then you meet the bean plant and the bacteria in her roots, who together pull nitrogen out of the air and leave a field richer than before. You also learn why farmers across India follow rice with a pulse.
intro.art: A child's hand dipping the corner of a dry cloth into a steel bowl of water, with a dark wet line climbing up the cloth, and a pot of soil with a mulch of dry leaves beside the bowl.

outcomes: I can explain why sand drains fast, clay holds water and loam does both well, using the size of the grains and the gaps between them.
I can show that water climbs through the gaps in soil against gravity, and say why finer grains lift water higher but more slowly.
I can explain how mulch and loosened soil change how fast a field loses water to the air.
I can say what nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium do for a plant, and what a fertiliser bag label means.
I can explain how bean plants and the bacteria in their root nodules pull nitrogen out of the air, and why farmers rotate pulses with cereals.
I can explain how irrigation can leave salt in a field, what salt does to seeds, and how some crops cope with it.
I can read a simple soil card and suggest what a field needs, and say how people found out that soil is not just crumbled rock.

terms.meaning: How coarse or fine a soil feels, decided by how much sand, silt and clay it has.
terms.example: A soil that feels gritty has a sandy texture. A soil that feels sticky when wet has a clayey texture.
terms.art: Three palms holding sand, pot soil and wet clay, each with a label for how it feels.

terms.meaning: A soil with a good mix of sand, silt, clay and humus. It drains well and still holds water that roots can use.
terms.example: Many vegetable gardens and fruit orchards are planted in loam.
terms.art: A cut-away of a garden bed with dark crumbly loam, roots running through it and a worm in a gap.

terms.meaning: A tiny gap between the grains in soil. Pores hold air and water.
terms.example: When you pour water on dry soil, bubbles pop out of the pores.
terms.art: A zoomed-in drawing of soil grains with the gaps between them in light blue and light grey.

terms.meaning: How fast extra water runs down and out of soil.
terms.example: Water runs out of a sandy pot in seconds, but a clayey pot stays wet for hours.
terms.art: Two flower pots being watered, one with water pouring from the bottom hole and one with a puddle on top.

terms.meaning: The climbing of water up through very narrow gaps, such as the gaps between soil grains or the threads of a cloth.
terms.example: Tea climbs up a sugar cube dipped in it, and oil climbs up the wick of a lamp.
terms.art: A cube of sugar with the corner dipped in tea and the brown stain climbing the cube.

terms.meaning: Water turning into an invisible gas and rising into the air.
terms.example: Wet clothes dry on a line because the water in them evaporates.
terms.art: A wet shirt on a line with wavy lines rising from it into the sunlight.

terms.meaning: A cover of straw, dry leaves, husk or similar material laid on top of soil to slow down evaporation.
terms.example: Farmers lay paddy straw or sugarcane leaves between rows of vegetables.
terms.art: A vegetable bed in a line of rows, with golden straw laid between the rows and damp dark soil showing where the straw is lifted.

terms.meaning: When a plant droops because her cells have lost water.
terms.example: A tomato plant in a pot droops in the afternoon sun when the soil is dry.
terms.art: A drooping tomato plant on one side of the picture and the same plant upright after watering on the other.

terms.meaning: A gas that makes up about four fifths of the air. It is also a nutrient that plants need to make leaves and grow green.
terms.example: A plant short of nitrogen has pale, yellowish leaves.
terms.art: A pie circle of air, mostly one colour labelled nitrogen, with a small slice labelled oxygen.

terms.meaning: A material that farmers add to soil to give plants nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
terms.example: Urea is a common fertiliser that holds a lot of nitrogen.
terms.art: A farmer scattering white grains from a bag on young green rice plants.

terms.meaning: A plant from the bean family, whose seeds grow in pods. Many legumes are pulses and can work with bacteria to take nitrogen from the air.
terms.example: Moong, urad, chana, groundnut and peas are legumes.
terms.art: A line of five legume plants with pods: moong, urad, chana, groundnut and pea.

terms.meaning: A small round swelling on the root of a legume, where helper bacteria live.
terms.example: On a pulled-up groundnut plant, the nodules look like tiny beads on the roots.
terms.art: A pulled-up bean plant with white soil-brown roots and small round bumps on the roots, one cut open to show a pink inside.

terms.meaning: Changing nitrogen gas from the air into a form that plants can use. Some bacteria can do this work. People can do it in factories.
terms.example: Bacteria in a bean's root nodules fix nitrogen.
terms.art: Air nitrogen going into a root nodule as two joined dots and coming out as a loose useful nitrogen taken up by the plant.

terms.meaning: Growing different crops one after another in the same field, instead of the same crop every time.
terms.example: A farmer grows rice, then black gram, then rice again.
terms.art: Four fields in a circle, each with a different crop, with arrows showing the order year by year.

terms.meaning: A field that is left without a crop for a season, to rest.
terms.example: In dry regions, farmers may leave a field fallow so its water can build up.
terms.art: A bare ploughed field in the morning mist, with a few weeds and a cow grazing, next to a green field.

terms.meaning: How much salt there is in soil or water.
terms.example: Seawater has high salinity. Rainwater has almost none.
terms.art: A white crust of salt on the surface of a dry field next to a bucket of seawater.

terms.meaning: Words for two opposite kinds of liquid or soil. Vinegar is acidic. Baking soda in water is alkaline. A soil may be one or the other, or neither.
terms.example: Tea grows best in acidic soil, and many chalky soils are alkaline.
terms.art: A row of three glass tumblers: pink cabbage water with vinegar, purple plain cabbage water and green-blue cabbage water with baking soda.

terms.meaning: Growing two or more crops together in the same field in the same season.
terms.example: Many farmers in Karnataka grow ragi with a row of red gram in between.
terms.art: A field with rows of ragi and a row of tall red gram plants between them.

explanations.concept: Texture decides how soil behaves with water
explanations.definition: A soil's texture is how much sand, silt and clay it has. The size of the grains decides how much water the soil holds and how fast it lets go.
explanations.description: Water in soil does not sit in puddles between the grains. Most of it clings to the grains as thin films. The finer the grains, the more grain surface there is for water to cling to. A few grams of some clays have more grain surface than a classroom floor. So clay holds a lot of water, and holds it tightly. But its gaps are tiny, so water drains very slowly, and when the soil is soaked there is little air left for roots. Sand is the other way round. Its gaps are big, so water runs through quickly and air gets in, but very little water stays behind. Loam has some of each, so it drains well and still keeps a lot of water that roots can use.
examples: A sandy pot dries out in a day in summer and needs watering often.
A field of heavy clay stays sticky and waterlogged after rain, and roots can struggle for air.
Coconut palms on the sandy coast of Kerala and Tamil Nadu need plenty of water because sand holds so little.
explanations.art: Three jars side by side: coarse sand with big gaps and water draining fast, clay with tiny gaps holding water, and loam in between, with a plant root in each.
explanations.context: Why do pots of sand, clay and garden soil behave so differently when watered? This card explains it.

explanations.concept: Water in soil: drains away, held for roots, held too tightly
explanations.definition: Water in soil comes in three kinds: water that drains away, water that roots can use, and water held so tightly by the finest grains that roots cannot pull it out.
explanations.description: After heavy rain, soil is full. The water in the biggest gaps runs down and drains away because of gravity. What is left is held on the grains as films. Roots can drink most of this water. But a small part sits so close to the finest grains that it is held very tightly, and roots cannot get it out. When the soil has dried down to that point, a plant droops, even though the soil still has a little water in it. This is called wilting. The best soil for a crop is one that, after the rain, keeps a lot of the second kind of water. Loam does that best. Sand has little of it, and clay holds a lot of the third kind.
examples: A sandy soil may need watering every day, because most of the water drains away and little is held for roots.
A potted plant drooping at midday and standing up again in the evening has used up the easy water and is waiting for more.
A farmer waters a field after the soil has begun to dry, not while it is still full, so the roots also get air.
explanations.art: A soil cross-section showing three sorts of water in three colours: water draining down through big gaps, water as a thin film around grains with a root hair drinking it, and water pressed tight to a clay flake.
explanations.context: How can a soil have water in it and still not give any to a plant? This card explains the three kinds of water in soil.

explanations.concept: Capillary rise: how water climbs through soil
explanations.definition: Capillary rise is water climbing up through very narrow gaps against gravity. The narrower the gap, the higher the water climbs.
explanations.description: Water is sticky in two ways. Water particles stick to each other, and they stick to the surface of the grains. At the edge of a narrow gap, the water sticks to the wall and pulls the water behind it upwards. This goes on until the weight of the lifted water balances the pull. In a wide gap, the pull is small, so water climbs only a little. In a narrow gap, the pull is strong, so water climbs much higher. It also moves more slowly through narrow gaps, because the gap is tight. So water climbs only a centimetre or two in gravel, tens of centimetres in sand, and up to a metre or more in very fine soil in the ground. But the finer the soil, the slower the climb. A cup of sand fills quickly, and a cup of fine soil takes much longer to wet. This is why a wick lifts oil up a diya, and why a sugar cube turns brown when you touch it to tea.
examples: Water climbs up the threads of a dry towel hanging with one corner in a bucket.
A mud wall of a house gets damp at the bottom after the rains, as water climbs up from the wet ground.
A cotton wick lifts oil up from the bowl of a lamp to the flame.
explanations.art: Three thin glass tubes standing in water, wide, medium and narrow, with the water climbing highest in the narrow tube, and beside them a cup of sand and a cup of fine soil.
explanations.context: Water went up a cloth with nobody pushing it. How? This card explains capillary rise.

explanations.concept: Why the top of a field dries, and what mulch does
explanations.definition: Soil loses most of its water to the air by evaporation from the top. Mulch, a cover of straw or leaves, slows this down.
explanations.description: Water climbs up through the soil by capillary rise until it reaches the surface. There the Sun and wind turn it into vapour and carry it away. On a hot day a bare field can lose a thick layer of water this way. A cover of straw, dry leaves or husk shades the soil and stops the wind from reaching it, so much less water escapes. Mulch also stops raindrops from beating the soil hard, and, as it rots, it turns into humus. Some farmers also loosen the top few centimetres of soil with a hoe. This is meant to break the narrow paths that the water climbs, so it is not drawn all the way up to the surface. Scientists find that this works well in some soils and little in others.
examples: Farmers lay paddy straw, coconut husk or sugarcane leaves around the plants in vegetable and banana fields.
A gardener covers the soil of a pot with dry leaves to keep it damp.
A black plastic sheet laid over soil, used on many farms, keeps the soil damp and the weeds down.

perspectives.explanation: Hoeing the top of the soil in a dry spell saves water, because it breaks the paths that carry water to the surface.
Loosening the soil helps in some soils and in some weather, but it can also dry out the top layer and bring more soil to the air. A cover of mulch works better in most tests.

explanations.art: Two soil beds in the Sun: a bare one with arrows of vapour rising and a pale dry top, and one covered in straw with dark damp soil underneath and few arrows.
explanations.context: Why does the top of bare soil dry out so fast? This card explains evaporation and mulch.

explanations.concept: What plants take from the soil: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium
explanations.definition: Plants make their food from air, water and light. But they also need more than a dozen nutrients from the soil. The three needed in the largest amounts are nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
explanations.description: A plant takes these nutrients through their roots, dissolved in water. Nitrogen goes into leaves and proteins, and gives leaves their green colour. A plant short of nitrogen has pale yellow leaves and grows slowly. Phosphorus helps roots grow, and helps flowers and seeds form. Potassium helps a plant manage her water and fight disease. Every harvest carries nutrients away from the field in the grain, the fruit and the stalks. So they must be put back. Farmers do this with compost, manure and fertilisers. A fertiliser bag shows three numbers for nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Urea has 46 per cent nitrogen, so 100 kilograms of urea carries 46 kilograms of nitrogen. A plant cannot tell whether a nitrate ion came from manure or from a factory. The ion is the same.
examples: A pale yellow rice field often means the plants are short of nitrogen.
The numbers on a bag of complex fertiliser, such as 19:19:19, are the shares of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
The Soil Health Card tells a farmer whether the soil is low, medium or high in each of these.
explanations.art: A young plant with three arrows from the roots labelled N for leaves, P for roots and flowers, K for water and health, beside a fertiliser bag showing three numbers.
explanations.context: Plants make their own food, so why do farmers spread fertiliser? This card explains what plants take from the soil.

explanations.concept: Nitrogen from the air: the bean and the bacteria
explanations.definition: Most plants cannot use the nitrogen gas in the air. Legumes can, because bacteria living in swellings on their roots change nitrogen gas into a form the plant can use.
explanations.description: About four of every five parts of air are nitrogen gas. Yet plants cannot use it, because the two nitrogen atoms in each molecule are held together very strongly. Some bacteria have a tool that can break that hold. Bean plants and their relatives have learned to house these bacteria. Rhizobium bacteria enter the root hairs of a young legume. The root grows a nodule around them. Inside, the bacteria change nitrogen gas into ammonia, which the plant turns into protein. The plant pays for this with sugar made in her leaves. Breaking the nitrogen bond takes a lot of energy. The tool the bacteria use is damaged by oxygen, so the nodule makes a red-pink substance that holds oxygen back. A working nodule is pink when you cut it open. Lightning also fixes a little nitrogen, and so do bacteria that live free in the soil. Rice farmers in India grow a floating fern called azolla in paddy fields, where blue-green bacteria in the fern leaves fix nitrogen.
examples: Moong, urad, groundnut, chana and peas all grow nodules on their roots.
A working nodule is pink inside, and one that has stopped working is white or green.
Azolla in a paddy field is a fern whose leaves hold nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a bean root: nitrogen gas as paired dots going down from the air into a round root nodule with a pink inside, ammonia moving up into the plant and sugar moving down to the bacteria.
explanations.context: How does a bean get nitrogen from the air when other plants cannot? This card explains the bean and the bacteria.

explanations.definition: Crop rotation is growing different crops in turn in the same field. It spreads out the work on the soil, and breaks up the life cycles of pests and diseases.
explanations.description: A crop of rice or wheat takes a lot of nitrogen out of the soil. A crop of moong or groundnut can fix its own nitrogen, so it takes less from the soil. The roots and leaves left behind in the field when a legume is harvested add nitrogen too, as they rot. This is why farmers have long followed a cereal with a pulse. But a pulse harvest also carries away nitrogen in its seeds, so the gain is smaller than many people think. Rotation also helps in other ways. A pest or disease that attacks one crop starves when the next crop is a different kind. Deep roots and shallow roots take water and nutrients from different layers. In the Kaveri delta, many farmers sow black gram or green gram on the damp soil left after the rice harvest. Some fields are also left fallow for a season, so the soil can rest and its water can build up.
examples: Rice then black gram, then rice again.
Groundnut then ragi, a pattern followed in many places in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
Cotton then a pulse, so the soil is not asked for the same thing twice in a row.
explanations.art: A circle of four fields labelled rice, black gram, rice and fallow, with arrows showing the order, and small nitrogen drops going into the soil under the black gram.
explanations.context: Why do farmers not grow the same crop in the same field every season? This card explains crop rotation.

explanations.concept: Growing crops together: intercropping and mixed fields
explanations.definition: Intercropping is growing two or more crops together in the same field. Crops that need different things, or that help each other, can share one field.
explanations.description: A tall crop and a short crop use light at different heights. A deep-rooted crop and a shallow-rooted one use water from different layers. A pulse grown between rows of cereal adds nitrogen near its neighbours. If one crop fails, another may still give a harvest. Many Indian farmers grow ragi with red gram, or groundnut with red gram. In Uttarakhand, the baranaja system grows around a dozen grains and pulses together. In North America, the Haudenosaunee peoples grew maize, beans and squash together: the maize stalk held the bean, the bean added nitrogen, and the squash leaves shaded the ground. The gain depends on the crops, and some mixes do worse than separate fields.
examples: Ragi with rows of red gram in Karnataka.
Coconut palms with banana, pepper and turmeric growing under them in Kerala.
Maize, beans and squash planted together by the Haudenosaunee.

perspectives.who: Many traditional farmers and some researchers
perspectives.explanation: A mixed field is steadier. If rain fails or a pest strikes one crop, the others still give a harvest.
One crop in a field is easier to plough, sow and harvest with machines, and gives a bigger harvest of that crop. Mixed fields can give a smaller total for the work, unless the farmer plans them well.

explanations.art: A mixed field in three layers: tall maize stalks with bean vines climbing them, and broad squash leaves on the ground below, with roots shown at three depths.
explanations.context: Why do some farmers grow several crops in one field? This card explains intercropping.

explanations.definition: Salt builds up in soil when water that carries salt is used up by evaporation and plants, and the salt is left behind.
explanations.description: All water from rivers, canals and wells carries a little dissolved salt. When this water is spread on a field and evaporates, only the water goes into the air. The salt stays. Year after year, it builds up, and in dry places a white crust can appear on the top of the soil. Salt makes it harder for roots to take in water, and too much damages them. Seeds sprout badly in salty soil. Salt also arrives where seawater creeps into the ground along a coast. Farmers can clear it by letting extra water wash the salt down and out through drains. Some crops have learned to cope. In Kerala, the Pokkali rice grown in the backwaters of Alappuzha and Ernakulam can grow in salty water. Millions of hectares of farmland around the world are damaged by salt.
examples: A white crust on the edge of a dry irrigated field.
A well along a coast turning brackish when too much groundwater is pumped out and seawater flows in.
Pokkali rice growing in the salty backwaters of Kerala.
explanations.art: A dry field with a white salt crust on top, irrigation water running in at one side and vapour rising, and a small salty drain at the far end.
explanations.context: Why can watering a field for years make the soil worse? This card explains how salt builds up.

explanations.definition: Soil can be acidic, neutral or alkaline. Plants grow best in different kinds, and each kind changes which nutrients a plant can take up.
explanations.description: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. A pH of 7 is neutral. Lower numbers are acidic, and higher numbers are alkaline. Vinegar is acidic. Baking soda in water is alkaline. Soils in rainy places, such as the laterite soils of Kerala, tend to be acidic, because rain washes away the minerals that balance acid. Soils in dry places, or made from chalky rock, tend to be alkaline. Tea bushes in Assam and the Nilgiris grow best in acid soil. In soil that is too acidic or too alkaline, some nutrients are locked up and a plant cannot take them in. A farmer can add lime to an acidic soil, and compost helps many soils. A Soil Health Card reports the pH of a field.
examples: Tea gardens in the Nilgiris and Assam grow on acid soils.
Red cabbage water turns pink with vinegar and green-blue with baking soda, and can be used to compare soils.
A farmer spreads lime on an acid field before sowing.
explanations.art: A pH scale as a colour strip from red acid on the left to purple neutral in the middle to blue-green alkaline on the right, with a tea bush at the acid end and a chalky field at the alkaline end.
explanations.context: Soils can be acidic or alkaline. What does that mean for plants? This card explains.

explanations.concept: Who is in charge of the trade between a bean and her bacteria?
explanations.description: The bean gives sugar. The bacteria give nitrogen. But what happens when some bacteria give less than others? In 2003, researchers reported that soybean plants seemed to punish nodules that fixed little nitrogen, perhaps by cutting their oxygen supply, and those bacteria did less well. Many biologists read this as the plant sanctioning cheats. Others say there is no plan behind it. The plant simply gives more oxygen and sugar to the nodules that are working, as a result of how the nodule is built. Some scientists point out that the bacteria also change their behaviour, and that bacteria in the soil sense chemicals and choose where to swim. So the trade may be steered from both sides. Nobody has settled how much choice each side has.
examples: A soybean nodule that fixes less nitrogen gets less oxygen.
Different kinds of Rhizobium bacteria can enter the same bean, and some fix more than others.
Beans in rich soil with plenty of nitrogen grow fewer nodules.

perspectives.explanation: The plant rewards nodules that give her nitrogen and punishes those that do not, like a trader who stops buying from a poor supplier. Cheating bacteria do worse.
Nothing is being decided. The nodule's oxygen and sugar supply simply follows how well the nodule is working, as the result of its build. Words like punish and reward are pictures.
Both sides sense and respond. A root hair curls around the bacteria that the plant accepts, and bacteria swim towards the signals the root sends. The trade is a conversation, not an order.

explanations.art: Two hands exchanging a sugar cube and a small nitrogen drop at a nodule in a bean root, with a question mark above.
explanations.context: Does a bean choose her bacteria? Scientists disagree, and this card gives their views.

explanations.concept: Nitrogen from factories, and what nobody knows yet
explanations.definition: In 1909 the German chemist Fritz Haber found a way to make ammonia from nitrogen gas and hydrogen, and Carl Bosch turned it into a factory process a few years later. Nitrogen fertiliser made this way is reported to feed about half the world's people today.
explanations.description: The Haber-Bosch process breaks the strong bond in nitrogen gas using high pressure and heat, and a metal catalyst. It uses a great deal of energy, which today mostly comes from natural gas and coal. The nitrogen that crops do not take up can wash into rivers and lakes. It feeds green algae, which then use up the oxygen in the water and kill fish. So scientists are asking new questions. Could cereals like rice and wheat be helped to grow their own nitrogen partners? A maize variety grown by the Mixe people in Oaxaca, Mexico, has been reported to grow root-like structures that drip a sugary jelly where nitrogen-fixing bacteria live. Can that be copied into other crops? Nobody knows yet whether it can be made to work at scale.
examples: A fertiliser factory turning nitrogen gas and hydrogen into ammonia.
Green algae covering a lake after nitrogen washes in from fields.
Researchers studying nitrogen-fixing bacteria on the aerial roots of the Oaxaca maize.
explanations.art: A fertiliser factory with tall pipes on one side and a bean field with nodules on the other, with a question mark above a rice plant growing its own tiny nitrogen helpers.
explanations.context: Where does most of the nitrogen in our food come from, and what might change? This card goes to the edge of what is known.

agreed.text: Water is held in soil as thin films on the grains and in the gaps, and finer soils hold more water.
agreed.evidence: Soil scientists weigh soils at known wetness and measure how much water they hold. Clay soils hold more than sand, in every measurement made.

agreed.text: Water climbs up through soil gaps against gravity, and finer gaps lift it higher but more slowly.
agreed.evidence: The climb has been measured in glass tubes and in soils for over a hundred years, and the height follows the width of the gap.

agreed.text: A cover of mulch cuts the water lost from the top of the soil.
agreed.evidence: Field trials in many countries, including India, weigh the water lost from mulched and bare soil. Mulched soil loses less.

agreed.text: Plants need nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in large amounts, and more than a dozen other nutrients in small amounts.
agreed.evidence: Plants grown in water with one nutrient left out show clear signs, such as pale leaves without nitrogen, and the signs go when the nutrient is added.

agreed.text: Bacteria in the nodules of legumes change nitrogen gas into ammonia, and the plant pays them in sugar.
agreed.evidence: Scientists give plants nitrogen gas with a marker form of nitrogen atom, and find the marker in the plant's proteins.

agreed.text: Irrigation water leaves its dissolved salt behind when it evaporates, and the salt can build up in the soil.
agreed.evidence: Salt crusts and measured salt levels are found in irrigated soils worldwide, and land managers have to wash the salt out.

agreed.text: Growing different crops in turn lowers the build-up of pests and diseases and spreads the demand on the soil.
agreed.evidence: Long-running field experiments, some over a hundred years old, compare fields with and without rotation.

challenging.claim: Sand is bad soil and clay is good soil, or the other way round.
challenging.who: A common idea among gardeners and farmers
challenging.for: Sand dries out fast, and clay can be sticky and hard to dig. Clay holds a lot of water and nutrients.
challenging.against: Each does some things well and some badly. Sand drains and has air, clay holds water and nutrients. Loam has some of each. What is good depends on the crop and the weather.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that one kind of soil is simply good and another bad.

challenging.claim: The more you water a plant, the better she grows.
challenging.for: A plant that wilts perks up when watered, so water seems to be the cure for everything.
challenging.against: Roots need air as well as water. In soil that is always soaked, the gaps fill with water and roots can rot. Both too little and too much water harm a plant.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that more water always helps.

challenging.who: Many people, and some bags and shops
challenging.for: Farmers say they feed the field, and plants grow faster after fertiliser.
challenging.against: Plants make their own food from air, water and light. Fertiliser gives the nutrients, such as nitrogen, that they need to build their bodies. It is more like the building material and vitamins than the meal.
challenging.context: This card is about whether fertiliser is food for plants.

challenging.claim: Natural manure is always better for the soil than factory fertiliser.
challenging.for: Manure and compost add humus, feed soil life and release nutrients slowly. Factory fertiliser used too much can wash into rivers.
challenging.against: A plant takes up the same nitrate ions from either. Manure alone often cannot supply enough nitrogen for high yields. Many soil scientists recommend using both, in the right amounts.
challenging.context: This card is about a long argument between organic and chemical farming.

challenging.claim: A crop of beans always leaves the soil richer in nitrogen.
challenging.for: Bean roots carry nitrogen-fixing bacteria, and fields after beans often grow better crops.
challenging.against: A harvest of bean seeds carries nitrogen away. If the whole plant is taken off the field, the soil may gain little or even lose nitrogen. The gain is greatest when the roots and leaves are left to rot in the field.
challenging.context: This card is about whether pulses always make the soil richer.

challenging.claim: A farmer who leaves a field fallow is wasting land.
challenging.who: Some city people, and some farmers under pressure
challenging.for: A field with no crop gives no food that season.
challenging.against: In dry regions, a fallow season lets rain water build up in the soil. It also lets weeds be ploughed in and pest cycles break. But a bare fallow is open to erosion, so it works best with a cover of plants or stubble. Where land is scarce, rotation with a pulse is often used in its place.
challenging.context: This card is about whether it is wise to leave a field resting.

big_questions.q: Water climbed up your cup of soil with nobody pushing it. What is doing the pulling?
big_questions.hint: Think about how water sticks to the grains, and what water is made of.

big_questions.q: A bean plant gives sugar to bacteria in her roots, and they give nitrogen back. Where did the energy in the sugar come from, and where does it go?
big_questions.hint: Follow the sugar back to the leaf, and the leaf back to the Sun.

big_questions.q: The air around you is about four fifths nitrogen, yet plants die of nitrogen hunger in a field. Why is plenty in the air not the same as plenty for the plant?

big_questions.q: A bean and her bacteria cannot grow nodules alone. Is the nodule part of the bean, part of the bacteria, or something new?

big_questions.q: Factories now make nitrogen fertiliser that helps feed about half the people on Earth. What would your town eat if the factories stopped?

story.title: Pink Inside the Knot
story.note: The story is made up. The farming in it is real. Black gram sown on the damp soil after a rice harvest is common in parts of the Kaveri delta. A working nodule is pink inside. A bean crop gives modest gains, and most farmers still use some fertiliser as well.
text: Karthika was ten years old, and she lived in a village near Kumbakonam, in the Kaveri delta. Her mother, Kamala, grew rice on two acres of flat green land. Her grandmother, Paati, lived with them, and so did her small brother Selvam, who was six and asked a question about everything.
The harvest was over. The fields were golden stubble, and the soil was still damp and dark. Karthika walked along the bund with Selvam, kicking small stones into the channel.
"Look," said Selvam. "Our field is yellow, and Murugan Mama's field is green."

He was right. In the last two seasons, the rice on their field had come up thin and pale. The leaves were the colour of old lemons. Murugan Mama ran the fertiliser shop at the bus stand, and his own land was dark green from edge to edge.
That evening, Murugan Mama came to the house. He put a white bag on the step. "Urea," he said. "You need more of it, Kamala akka. Put it on the day you plant. Your soil is hungry."
"I know it is hungry," said Kamala. She rubbed her forehead. "But a bag of urea costs a lot of money."

Paati had been listening from her cot. "When your grandfather farmed this land," she said, "I scattered ulundu seeds on the wet soil, the week after the cutting. Black gram, you call it. We pulled the pods, and we gave the rest of the plants back to the soil. We never bought a bag of anything. Our rice was green."
"That was long ago, Amma," said Kamala. "There is no time for it now."
Murugan Mama laughed kindly. "A pulse is a waste of a season. The soil takes, you know. The soil is a bank. When the bank is empty, you must put money in. Urea is the money."

Karthika was thinking about her science lesson on yellow leaves. Her teacher had said that pale yellow leaves often mean a plant is short of nitrogen. But the air was full of nitrogen. Her teacher had said that too. About four of every five parts of air are nitrogen gas. So why did the rice go hungry with all that nitrogen around her?

She decided to look at the ulundu. Paati kept a tin of seeds under her bed. Karthika scattered a handful along the damp edge of the field, as Paati showed her, and they sprouted in four days. Three weeks later, the small plants were knee-high and covered in flowers.
She asked Paati to pull one up. Selvam shouted before anyone else did. "She has beads on her roots! Little white beads!"
Karthika washed the roots in the channel. Along them sat small round bumps, each about as big as a sesame seed. They were smooth and hard. "What are they?" she asked.
Paati shrugged. "Pearls, my mother used to say. The ulundu always has them."
Karthika took the plant to the kitchen. With her mother standing beside her, she cut one bump in half with the small vegetable knife. Selvam leaned in so close that his nose almost touched it.
"It is pink," he whispered. "Like the inside of a guava."

It was pink all through. Karthika remembered her teacher's words. A working nodule is pink inside. It holds bacteria that take nitrogen from the air and give it to the plant. She drew it in her notebook, and wrote under it: the bean does not only take. The bean gives.
"So," Kamala said slowly, "the ulundu has tiny helpers in her roots. They pull nitrogen from the air. When we plough the roots and leaves back in, the nitrogen stays in the field."
"And the rice gets it next season," said Karthika.

That season, Kamala sowed ulundu on half of her field and left the other half bare. The rest of the plants were ploughed back in after the pods were picked. In the next rice season, she bought a smaller bag of urea for the whole field, and put it on evenly.

Two months later, the rice on the ulundu half stood a little darker than the rice on the other half. It was not a huge difference, but anyone could see the line down the middle of the field. Murugan Mama came to look, with his hands behind his back.
"The beans have been paying rent in nitrogen all this time," he said at last. "And I told you the soil was a bank."
"It is a bank," said Karthika. "But something is also putting money in. The bacteria in the beans are the ones doing it."

Murugan Mama took a handful of ulundu seeds from Paati's tin. He said they were for his own field, and that he would try just a small corner. Then he looked at Selvam, who was staring at him with great interest.
"What?" said Murugan Mama.
"Can I cut one open?" said Selvam.
story.epiphany: For the parent: nitrogen is a gas that makes up about four fifths of air, but plants cannot use it as a gas. Bacteria in the nodules of legumes break the strong bond between the two nitrogen atoms and make ammonia, and the plant pays with sugar. Karthika's pink nodule was a working one. The bean crop did not make the field rich in one season, which is why the gain in the story is modest and the farmer still uses some urea. The key was seeing that a plant can give to the soil as well as take, with the help of another kind of living being.
ask: Why was the rice on the field pale yellow, and what did the ulundu plants do about it?
What did Karthika see inside the cut nodule, and what did the colour tell her?
Murugan Mama called the soil a bank. In what way is that a good picture, and in what way does the bean change it?
Why did Kamala plough the roots and leaves back into the field after picking the pods?
Paati and her mother knew that ulundu helped the rice, long before anyone had seen a nodule. How did they know?

roots.context: We have watched water climb through soil, saved water with a cover of leaves, and met the bacteria in a bean's roots. Now we ask what a bean, a field and a bag of urea tell us about how life is fed.

deep_truth.truth: Beans do not only take from a field. Tiny bacteria in swellings on their roots pull nitrogen out of the air, and the bean pays them in sugar. So a bean's food is made by two kinds of life working together. That is why a field can end a season richer than it began.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a plant as one being on her own, and of soil as a bank that she empties and a farmer refills. A nodule is part bean and part bacteria, and the giving goes both ways.
deep_truth.evidence: A working nodule is pink inside. Farmers in the Kaveri delta sow black gram after rice, and the next rice often grows greener. Scientists who feed beans nitrogen gas marked with a rare kind of atom find the marked atoms in the bean's protein.

three.who_am_i: The protein in your dal was nitrogen gas in the air, until bacteria in a bean's roots turned it into something a plant can use. Your body then built it into you.
three.what_is_life: A bean and her bacteria are two different kinds of life, and neither does well alone. A great deal of life is made of partnerships like this one.
three.what_is_this_world: Nitrogen passes from air to bacteria to bean to person to soil and back to the air. A field is a place where a stream flows through, not a store that empties.

roots.thread: The nitrogen in the air, the sugar in a bean leaf, the bacteria in a root and the dal on your plate look like four separate things. They are one stream. Sunlight makes the sugar, the sugar pays the bacteria, the bacteria turn air into protein, and a family eats the protein. Then bodies and roots and leaves return the nitrogen to the soil, and the stream begins again. No step in the chain can do it alone.

teachings.teaching: From food, living beings come into being. From rain, food is born.
teachings.link: The verse follows the chain backwards from the body to the rain. This unit adds two more links in the chain: the soil that holds the rain, and the bacteria that put nitrogen into the food.

teachings.teaching: Nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water, yet nothing is better at wearing down the hard and the strong.
teachings.link: Water is soft, yet it climbs through a cup of fine grains against gravity, and it dissolves the salt and the nutrients that roots need.

teachings.source: Avatamsaka Sutra, the image of Indra's net
teachings.teaching: Every jewel in a great net reflects every other jewel, so each one holds all the others.
teachings.link: A nodule is a place where a plant, a bacterium, the air and the Sun all meet, and each is needed for the pink inside.

science.text: Bacteria in the root nodules of legumes change nitrogen gas into ammonia, and the plant pays them with sugar.
Whether a bean plant chooses her bacteria, or the match simply follows from how the nodule is built, is argued about by biologists.

other_view.view: A nodule is an organ built by the plant using her own genes, and the bacteria are workers inside the nodule. Calling the two a partnership of equals is a picture. The bean grows nodules when she needs nitrogen, and stops when she does not.

practice.title: Watch the cloth drink
practice.say: Fold a strip of cloth or kitchen tissue and hang one end in a glass of water. Sit and watch the water climb. Breathe in slowly three times, and let the breath out gently. With each breath, notice the wet line moving a little higher. Nobody is pushing it. When you are ready, think of the same thing happening under every field.
practice.kid: Hang one end of a strip of cloth in water. Watch the wet line climb. Breathe in slowly three times. Nobody is pushing it.

games.title: Soil Bank: a game of crops and nitrogen
games.context: This is a card game. Each player runs a field for eight seasons. Some crops take nitrogen out of the soil, and some put it back. The player who earns the most harvest points wins.

printables.title: 30 nitrogen tokens, small paper squares marked N (dry beans or buttons will do instead)
Score sheet for one field
items: Season 1 to 8: the crop played, the nitrogen bank after the season, the points

rules: Each player has a field. Draw a circle on a sheet of paper and call it the nitrogen bank. Put 4 nitrogen tokens in it. Put the rest of the tokens in the middle as the supply. If the supply runs out of tokens, use dry beans or buttons from a bowl.
Shuffle the crop cards and deal 3 to each player. Put the rest face down as a pile. If the pile runs out, shuffle the played cards and use them as a new pile.
A game has 8 seasons. In each season, every player plays one card face up on their field.
A card that says Needs asks you to pay that many tokens from your bank to the supply. If your bank has fewer, the crop fails. Pay what you have and score 0 for the season.
A card that says Gives lets you take that many tokens from the supply into your bank. A fallow card also gives 1 token, but no points.
If you play the same crop as the last card in your own field, pests spread. Take away 2 points from that card.
At the end of every season, each player takes 1 token from the supply for rain, fallen leaves and the bacteria in the soil. Then everyone draws back up to 3 cards.
After season 8, add up your points. The highest score wins. Playing alone, try to score 30 or more, and beat your own score next time. Two to four players is best.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and tokens. Draw a nitrogen bank circle for each player. Put 4 tokens in each bank. Deal 3 cards each.
flow.say: We are farmers for eight seasons. Each of us has a field with a bank of nitrogen. Some crops spend the bank. Some fill it up.
flow.kid: Make your bank circle. Put in 4 tokens. Take 3 cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Soil Bank, a card game about crops and nitrogen.

flow.do: Play one practice season together. Each player picks one card, plays it, pays or takes the tokens, and scores.
flow.say: Read your card. If it says Needs, pay tokens from your bank. If it says Gives, take tokens. Then write your points.
flow.kid: Play one card. Pay or take tokens. Write your points.

ask.q: Which of your cards will use up the most nitrogen?
good: Sugarcane.
Rice or wheat.
The ones that say Needs 3.

flow.parent: Let your child read the cards aloud. Help with the paying and taking until the rules are clear. The practice season counts.

flow.do: Play seasons 2, 3 and 4. After every season, everyone takes 1 token for rain and draws back up to 3 cards.
flow.say: Look at your bank before you choose. Can your field pay for the crop you want?
flow.kid: Look at your bank. Pick a card you can pay for.

check.q: Your bank is empty and you hold Rice, Moong and Sugarcane. Which card is the best to play?
options: Rice
Sugarcane
Moong
check.why: With an empty bank, rice and sugarcane would fail, so you would score nothing and gain nothing. Moong gives 2 tokens and scores 2 points, and it fills the bank for the next season.

flow.context: In this step you play the first seasons of the game and learn to look at your nitrogen bank before you pick a crop.

flow.do: Stop after season 4. Look at every bank. Compare the banks of players who played only cereals with the banks of players who mixed in pulses.
flow.say: Halfway through. Whose bank is fullest? Who played what? What do you notice?
flow.kid: Compare the banks. Whose is fullest? What did they play?

ask.q: What do the fullest banks have in common?
good: They played a pulse or fallow between the cereals.
They did not play rice every time.
They played crops that need little.

flow.parent: A good answer says that pulses and fallow refill the bank, and that the same crop twice in a row loses points. If a player did best with only cereals, check the season where they struggled.

flow.do: Play seasons 5, 6, 7 and 8. Keep taking 1 token at the end of each season and drawing back up to 3 cards.
flow.say: Four seasons left. Plan two seasons ahead. What will your bank hold in the next season?
flow.kid: Plan two seasons ahead. Keep your bank full.
flow.think: Is it better to score high now, or to fill the bank for later?

flow.do: Add up the points. Then talk about which plan scored best.
flow.say: Add up your points. Whose plan won? Why did the best fields not grow the same crop every season?
flow.kid: Add your points. What plan worked best? Why?

ask.q: Why do real farmers often follow a cereal with a pulse?
good: The pulse puts nitrogen back in the soil.
It saves money on fertiliser.
It breaks the life cycle of pests.

flow.parent: The game is a simple picture. In a real field the gains from a pulse are smaller than the game shows, and the bank also grows through manure and fertiliser.

Am I the capital of India?

Is it in the soil or in the air?
Is it a gas, a liquid or a solid?

experiments.title: Water Climb: how fast does water rise in gravel, sand and fine soil?
experiments.question: If three cups of dry gravel, sand and fine soil stand in a shallow tray of water, how high does the water climb in each one, and how fast?
experiments.predict: Look at the three dry materials. Which one will the water climb highest in? Which will it climb fastest in? Which will it not climb in at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three cups are the same size and are filled to the same line with dry material. Each is tapped five times on the table to settle it. All three stand in the same tray with the same depth of water at the same moment. Only the size of the grains changes, so any difference in the climb comes from the grains. Look at the same times for all three.
results_table: Gravel: height of the wet line (cm)
Sand: height of the wet line (cm)
Fine soil: height of the wet line (cm)

materials.item: three tall clear plastic cups of the same size, about 11 centimetres tall
a nail and a hammer or pliers, for a grown-up to make holes in the cups (or the point of a pair of scissors)
an old cotton cloth, cut into three small circles that cover the bottom of a cup
dry gravel, as small stones about the size of a pea, washed and dried
dry building sand, washed and dried in the Sun for a day before the test
dry garden or red soil from outside (not coco-peat potting mix, which repels water), crumbled and rubbed through a tea strainer to make it fine
a flat tray or a wide plate with a rim, and water
a small plate for looking at the dry materials
a few drops of food colour or blue ink (optional, it only makes the wet line easier to see), a ruler, a marker pen, a clock or phone timer

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the holes in the cups, because the nail is sharp. Rub the dry soil gently and do not breathe in the dust. Wash hands after touching soil. Do the hole-making over a towel, and keep the nail and scissors away from small children.

schedule.what: Look at the materials, guess, make the cups, fill them and start the water. Look at 5, 15, 30 and 60 minutes.
Look again the next morning and measure the final wet line.

experiments.record: Fill in the table at each time. Then draw the three cups with their wet lines at 60 minutes. Write which cup filled first and which did not fill.

flow.do: Spread a little of each dry material on a plate. Look closely and feel each one. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write it down.
flow.say: Here are gravel, sand and fine soil, all dry. We will stand each in a little water. How high will the water climb? How fast? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the three. Which will the water climb best? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will let the water climb best?
good: It has the most gaps.
It has the smallest grains.
Water goes where it is easiest.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children think that big gaps let water move best. The test will show that very big gaps are not best for climbing. One child with a parent: do every cup yourselves. Two to four children: each child makes and fills one cup (A, B or C, and a fourth child can repeat the sand), and all stand together in one tray. One child keeps the clock, one marks the lines, one writes the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Water Climb test. You look at three dry materials and guess before you test.

flow.do: Ask a grown-up to make five small holes in the bottom of each cup. Lay a cloth circle inside each cup. Draw a line every centimetre up the outside with the marker.
flow.say: Fine grains must not fall out of the holes, so the cloth goes in first. The lines on the side are our ruler.
flow.kid: Holes in the bottom. A cloth circle inside. Draw lines up the side.
flow.parent: The nail makes the holes. Press it through slowly, over a towel. The cloth stops the soil falling out but still lets water in. Mark the cups A for gravel, B for sand and C for fine soil.
flow.context: In this step you make three cups that can sit in water and show the wet line on their sides.

flow.do: Fill cup A with gravel, cup B with sand and cup C with fine soil, each to the 9 centimetre line. Tap each cup on the table five times. Top it up to the 9 centimetre line.
flow.say: Every cup is filled to the same line. Tap each cup the same number of times, so the grains settle the same way.
flow.kid: Fill to the 9 centimetre line. Tap five times. Top up.

check.q: Why do we fill all three cups to the same line and tap them five times?
options: So the cups look neat
So only the size of the grains is different
So the water has less to climb
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one cup were packed tighter or filled higher, you would not know whether the grains or the packing made the difference.

flow.context: In this step you fill three cups with the same height of dry material.

flow.do: Pour 1 centimetre of coloured water into the tray. Stand all three cups in it at the same moment. Start the clock.
flow.say: All three stand in the water together. Now watch the sides of the cups. Dark means wet.
flow.kid: Put all three in the water at once. Start the clock.
flow.parent: Stand the cups in the tray at the same moment. The water in the tray will go down as the cups drink it. Top it up to 1 centimetre when you check, and add the same water to the tray before you leave it overnight.
flow.context: In this step the three cups go into the water and the timing starts.

flow.do: Look at the cups after 5, 15, 30 and 60 minutes. Use the marker to draw a line at the top of the wet part each time. Write the heights in the table.
flow.say: How high is the wet line now in each cup? Which is climbing fastest? Is any cup not climbing?
flow.kid: Look at each cup. Mark the wet line. Write the heights.

ask.q: What do you see in the gravel cup, compared with the sand cup?
good: The water barely climbs in the gravel.
The sand is wet nearly to the top.
The gravel stays mostly dry.

flow.parent: Measure from the water level in the tray. Often the gravel wet line stays at about 1 to 2 centimetres. The sand rises quickly at first, often several centimetres in the first hour, and may reach the top by the next morning. The fine soil is slower to start, because it is dusty and takes time to wet. If the fine soil stays dry for a long time, write that down: it is a result too. If the soil floats a dry crust on top and nothing climbs, it may be potting mix with coco-peat that repels water: try plain garden soil. Times will be a little different in hot and in damp weather, so compare the three cups with each other, not with the example.
flow.wait: Leave the cups standing until the next morning.

flow.do: The next morning, measure the wet line in each cup. Write the heights in the last row of the table.
flow.say: It is the next day. Has the wet line in the fine soil caught up with the sand?
flow.kid: Measure the wet lines again. Has the fine soil caught up?
flow.parent: By the next morning the fine soil has often climbed much further than it had after an hour, perhaps to the top. Top up the tray water if it has gone dry overnight. If a wet line has reached the top of the cup, write: to the top.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you find? What did you see? Why do you think the grains made the difference?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I found. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the smaller the gaps, the stronger the pull on the water. What I saw: the gravel climbed about 1 centimetre, the sand climbed fast and the fine soil climbed slowly but kept going. Why: water sticks to the grains and pulls the water behind it up. Narrow gaps have more grain close to the water, so the pull is stronger. But narrow gaps are also harder to flow through, so the climb is slower.

check.q: The gravel cup stayed almost dry, and the sand cup was wet to the top. What does this show?
options: Gravel is heavier than sand
Very wide gaps cannot lift water far
Sand is made of water
check.why: Water is pulled up by its stickiness to the grains at the edges of a gap. In very wide gaps most of the water is too far from a grain to be pulled. In narrow gaps all the water is close to a grain, so it is lifted. Picking heavier gravel is a fair thought, but weight is not the cause.

flow.context: This step asks you to say what you found, what you saw and why. Scientists call it claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.context: In this experiment you stand cups of gravel, sand and fine soil in a tray of water. You watch how far and how fast the water climbs through the gaps between the grains.

experiments.title: Salty Seeds: how much salt stops moong from sprouting?
experiments.question: A pinch of salt, a spoon of salt or a lot of salt in the water: how much does it take to stop moong seeds from sprouting?
experiments.predict: Four saucers will have water with no salt, a little salt, more salt and a lot of salt. How many seeds will sprout in each? Which saucer will sprout first? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each saucer has 10 seeds from the same packet, the same kind of tissue and the same amount of liquid. All four sit in the same place. The only thing that changes is the amount of salt. Seeds are counted at the same time each day. The saucer with no salt shows how well the seeds sprout without any help or harm.
results_table: Saucer and salt in 100 millilitres of water
After rinsing in plain water: seeds sprouted by day 6

materials.item: four small plates or saucers
kitchen tissue or an old thin cotton cloth, enough to cover the bottom of each saucer in three layers
40 whole green moong seeds from the kirana, from one packet. Do not soak them first: the test is how salty water slows a dry seed taking in water. Not split moong dal
ordinary table salt (any kind) and a teaspoon
a medicine cup or measuring cup marked in millilitres, and a tablespoon (about 15 millilitres)
four cups or glasses to mix the salt waters in
a marker pen and four pieces of paper for labels

experiments.safety: Do not eat the soaked seeds, and do not taste the salty water. Wash your hands after touching the seeds. Keep the salty water away from your eyes and away from small children. Even though moong is food, do not eat these seeds, because they sit in salty water on tissue for days.

schedule.what: Make four salt waters. Put 10 dry seeds on wet tissue in each saucer.
Count the sprouted seeds (many may not have sprouted yet). Add a tablespoon of the right liquid to each saucer.
Count again and add liquid.
Count again. Rinse the seeds that have not sprouted and put them on plain wet tissue.
Count the rinsed seeds that have sprouted. Fill in the last column and talk about the results.

experiments.record: Fill in the table after each count. A seed has sprouted when a tiny white root is at least 2 millimetres long. Draw the four saucers on day 3.

flow.do: Show the four saucers and the salt. Say that the water will have different amounts of salt. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: Four saucers, four waters. One has no salt. One has a pinch. One has half a spoon. One has a whole spoon. How many seeds will sprout in each? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four waters with different salt. How many seeds sprout in each? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think salt might change how seeds sprout?
good: Salt is bad for plants.
Salt takes the water out of the seed.
Salt makes the water too heavy for the seed.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Sea water has about 6 level teaspoons of salt in a litre, which is a little more than saucer C holds in the same amount of water (about 5 teaspoons in a litre).
flow.context: This is the first step of the Salty Seeds test. You guess how salt changes sprouting before you test.

flow.do: Label the saucers A, B, C and D. Put 100 millilitres of water in four cups. Leave A plain. Stir one eighth of a level teaspoon of salt into B. Stir half a teaspoon into C. Stir one level teaspoon into D. Stir until the salt is gone.
flow.say: A is plain water. B has a pinch of salt. C has half a teaspoon. D has a whole teaspoon. C is nearly as salty as the sea.
flow.kid: Make four waters. A plain, B a pinch, C half a spoon, D a spoon.
flow.parent: Use a level spoon, not a heaped one. One eighth of a teaspoon is a small pinch. Keep the waters apart and label each cup so they do not get mixed. One child with a parent: make all four. Two to four children: each child makes and looks after one saucer, then you put the counts in one table. If you have only one child, the parent counts the seeds too, so the counting is checked.

check.q: Why is one saucer given plain water with no salt?
options: To show how the seeds sprout without any salt
To make the test longer
To have one saucer that looks different
check.why: The plain saucer is the comparison. If the seeds in plain water sprout well, then any seeds that do not sprout in the salty saucers fail because of the salt, and not because the seeds were old.

flow.context: In this step you make four waters with different amounts of salt.

flow.do: Lay three layers of tissue in each saucer. Pour 3 tablespoons of the right water into each saucer. Put 10 soaked seeds on each tissue, with space between them. Put a label on each saucer.
flow.say: Pour the right water into the right saucer. The tissue should be wet, with no puddle. Space the seeds apart, so you can count them.
flow.kid: Wet the tissue with the right water. Put 10 seeds on each.
flow.parent: The tissue should be damp, not floating. Put the saucers in a warm place away from direct sun. A kitchen shelf is good. In a very hot or dry room the tissue dries fast: cover each saucer loosely with an upturned plate and check each morning. In a cool room (below about 20 degrees) moong is slow, so count one day later. Moong in plain water should show a white root on most seeds by day 2 or 3. If fewer than 7 of 10 seeds in saucer A sprout, the seeds are old: start again with a fresh packet.

flow.do: After one day, count the seeds that have sprouted in each saucer. Write the numbers in the table. Add one tablespoon of the right water to each saucer.
flow.say: Count the sprouted seeds in each saucer. Which saucer is ahead?
flow.kid: Count the sprouted seeds. Write the numbers.

ask.q: Which saucer is ahead, and which is behind?
good: The plain one is ahead.
The saltiest one has no sprouts.
The pinch one is almost as good as the plain one.

flow.parent: Often the plain saucer has most seeds sprouted by day 2 or 3. The pinch saucer may be a little behind. The half-spoon saucer is usually slow and may have few or none, and the one-spoon saucer none at all. The exact numbers depend on the seeds. If all four look the same, write that down, and try fresh seeds. That is a real result too.

flow.do: On days 2 and 3, count the sprouted seeds again. Top up the right water each day. On day 4, take the seeds that have not sprouted out of the salty saucers. Rinse them in plain water. Put them on plain wet tissue.
flow.say: Now a second question. Salt held the seeds back. Did it kill them? Rinse them in plain water and wait two more days.
flow.kid: Rinse the seeds that have not sprouted. Put them on plain wet tissue.
flow.parent: Salt can hold seeds back or hurt them, depending on how salty it is. After a rinse, a few seeds from the middle saucers may sprout. Seeds from the saltiest saucer often do not, or do so only slowly. Count only roots that are at least 2 millimetres long. The salty seeds may smell or grow mould by day 4: throw them away if they do, and write that down. Write down whatever happens.
flow.wait: Wait two more days, then count the rinsed seeds.

flow.do: On day 6, count the rinsed seeds that have sprouted. Fill in the last column. Then ask for the three things: what I think, what I saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. How much salt did it take to stop the seeds? What did you see? Why does salt do this?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: more salt means fewer sprouted seeds. In the saltiest water, almost no seeds sprouted. Why: salty water holds on to its water very tightly, so the seed finds it hard to take water in. Too much salt can also harm the seed. Real fields work the same way. A field with a white salt crust grows poor crops.

check.q: A farmer's field has a white crust of salt on the top after many years of watering. Why are the seeds she sows there growing badly?
options: The salt makes it hard for seeds and roots to take in water
The salt makes the soil too cold
The salt feeds the seeds too much
check.why: Salty water holds on to its water tightly, so seeds and roots find it hard to drink. That is what happened in the salty saucers. Salt is not a food for plants, so more of it does not feed them more.

flow.context: This step asks you to say what you found, what you saw and why.

experiments.context: In this experiment you sprout moong seeds in plain water and in water with different amounts of salt. You find out how much salt stops seeds from sprouting.

experiments.title: Cover or Bare: does a cover of dry leaves keep the soil damp?
experiments.question: Two cups of the same damp soil sit in the same sunny window. One is covered with dry leaves and one is bare. Which dries out deeper in three days?
experiments.predict: Which cup will have a thicker dry layer at the top after three days? Will the cover of leaves make a difference? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both cups have the same soil, the same depth of soil, and the same amount of water poured in slowly. They sit side by side in the same sunny place. Only the leaf cover changes. We measure the pale dry layer at the same time each day.
results_table: Bare cup: thickness of the pale dry layer (mm)
Covered cup: thickness of the pale dry layer (mm)
Loosened cup: thickness of the pale dry layer (mm)

materials.item: three clear plastic cups of the same size
garden soil or red soil, enough to fill each cup to 6 centimetres, the same soil for all three, dry and crumbled (not coco-peat potting mix, which repels water and looks pale)
water and a tablespoon
dry leaves, straw or coconut husk, enough for a layer 2 centimetres thick
a fork, a ruler, a marker pen
a sunny windowsill or balcony ledge, and a kitchen scale in grams if you have one

schedule.what: Fill the cups, wet them, cover one and loosen the top of another. Put them in the sun.
Lift the cover aside and measure the pale dry layer in each cup.
Measure again.
Measure again, then talk about the results.

experiments.record: Fill in the table each day. Draw the three cups on day 4 with the dark damp soil and the pale dry layer.

flow.do: Show the three cups, the soil and the leaves. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write it down.
flow.say: Two cups of the same soil, in the same Sun. One gets a cover of dry leaves. Which dries out more? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two cups, one covered. Which dries out more? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the leaves will make a difference?
good: The leaves keep the Sun off the soil.
The leaves keep the wind away.
The leaves will soak up the water.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Some children think the leaves will soak up the water and make the soil drier.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cover or Bare test. You guess how a leaf cover changes the drying before you test.

flow.do: Fill each cup with soil to 6 centimetres. Pour 4 tablespoons of water slowly on each. Wait 10 minutes. Then lay 2 centimetres of dry leaves on one cup. Use the fork to loosen the top 2 centimetres of soil in another.
flow.say: Same soil, same water, same depth in each cup. One is bare, one is covered, and one has loose soil on top.
flow.kid: Fill the cups. Add water. Cover one. Loosen one.
flow.parent: Label the cups Bare, Covered and Loosened. The soil next to the clear wall will look dark when it is wet and pale when it is dry. If you have a kitchen scale, weigh each cup now and again each morning. The lighter the cup, the more water has gone. One child with a parent: one child sets all three cups. Two to four children: each child fills one cup, or each makes a full set of three and you compare sets. One child pours, one measures, one writes.

check.q: Why do we pour the same amount of water on each cup?
options: So that only the cover is different
So the soil gets cold
So the cups look the same
check.why: If one cup got more water, it would stay wet longer for that reason, and you could not tell whether the leaf cover made the difference.

flow.context: In this step you set up three cups of damp soil with different covers.

flow.do: Put the three cups side by side in the same sunny place. Do not move them.
flow.say: Same Sun, same wind. Now we wait one day.
flow.kid: Put the cups in the sun. Do not move them.
flow.wait: Leave the cups in the Sun until tomorrow.

flow.do: Each day, lift the leaves aside. Look at the soil next to the wall of each cup. Measure the thickness of the pale dry layer at the top with a ruler, in millimetres. Write it in the table. Put the leaves back.
flow.say: Look at the side of the cup. Dark soil is damp. Pale soil is dry. How thick is the pale layer at the top?
flow.kid: Look at the side. Measure the pale layer. Write it down.

ask.q: What is the difference between the bare cup and the covered cup?
good: The bare one has a thick dry layer.
The covered one is still dark.
The covered one dried less.

flow.parent: After a day or two in strong sun, the bare cup usually has a pale layer of a centimetre or more. The covered cup is usually still dark almost to the top. The loosened cup may be like the bare cup or may be a bit different, because the loose layer dries first. If the cups are alike, write that down: it is a result too. A damp, cloudy or monsoon week will make all the cups slow to dry: then measure for two more days, or stand the cups in a sunny, breezy place. If you have a scale, the weight lost each day is a second, clearer measurement.
flow.wait: Measure again tomorrow, and again on day 4.

flow.do: On day 4, measure for the last time. Then ask your child for the three things: what I think, what I saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did the leaves do? What did you see? Why do you think the covered soil stayed damp?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: a cover of leaves keeps soil damp for longer. The bare cup had a thick dry layer and the covered cup had almost none. Why: the leaves shade the soil and stop the wind, so less water turns into vapour and leaves. Farmers lay straw between rows for the same reason.

check.q: A gardener covers the soil of a pot with dry leaves in summer. What is she trying to do?
options: Slow down evaporation from the soil
Make the soil hotter
Stop the plant growing
check.why: The leaves shade the soil and stop the wind from reaching it, so less water escapes into the air. Mulch also breaks down into humus over time.

flow.context: This step asks you to say what you found, what you saw and why.

experiments.context: In this experiment you compare three cups of damp soil in the Sun, to see how a cover of leaves changes how fast the soil dries.

activities.title: Squeeze and Ribbon: how does each soil feel when wet?

materials.item: a spoon of clean building sand
a spoon of garden soil (any soil from outside, with the stones picked out)
a spoon of wet clay, such as potter's clay or multani mitti (Fuller's earth) mixed with water to a paste
a little water in a cup
a ruler and a notebook
a plate

activities.safety: Wash hands with soap after touching soil. Do not put soil or clay in your mouth.

schedule.what: Wet three soils to dough. Make a ball and a ribbon from each. Measure the ribbons.

activities.record: A table with three rows: sand, garden soil and clay. For each, write whether it made a ball, and how long the ribbon was.

flow.do: Put a spoon of each soil in its own spot on a plate. Add water a few drops at a time. Mix with a finger until each is like soft dough.
flow.say: Make each soil as wet as soft dough. Add the water a few drops at a time. If it is too wet, add a little more soil.
flow.kid: Wet each soil until it is like soft dough.

ask.q: Before you test them, which soil do you think will hold together best?
good: The clay.
The one that is stickiest.
The one with the finest grains.

flow.parent: Do not say which will hold together. Let the hands find out. If the clay is already a paste, use it as it is. One child with a parent: do all three yourselves, and let the parent do one too to compare hands. Two to four children: each child makes a set of three and you compare ribbon lengths on one table. The cup of water is shared; wash hands in a bowl, not the sink, because clay can block drains.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Squeeze and Ribbon test. You wet three soils to find out how each one feels.

flow.do: Take a lump of each soil the size of a marble. Squeeze it in your fist. Open your hand. Does it keep its shape? Press it gently with a finger. Does it crack or stay whole?
flow.say: Squeeze, then open your hand. Does the ball hold? Poke it gently. Does it crumble?
flow.kid: Squeeze a ball. Open your hand. Does it hold?
flow.parent: Sand falls apart and will not make a ball. Pot soil usually makes a ball that cracks when poked. Wet clay makes a smooth ball that does not crack.

flow.do: Take a lump of each soil. Press it between your thumb and first finger, pushing it forward into a flat strip. Let the strip hang over your finger. Measure it when it breaks.
flow.say: Push the soil forward between thumb and finger. Make a flat ribbon. How long can it get before it breaks?
flow.kid: Push a flat ribbon between thumb and finger. Measure it.
flow.parent: Sand makes no ribbon. Loam breaks at about 2 centimetres or less. Clay can make a ribbon 5 centimetres long or more, because the finest grains stick to each other. The lengths are a rough guide, because the wetness changes the result.

check.q: A soil makes a long smooth ribbon when wet. What does this say about the soil?
options: It has a lot of clay in it
It is mostly sand
It has no water in it
check.why: Clay grains are the smallest and stickiest, so they hold together in a long ribbon. Sand grains are too big and smooth to stick, so a sandy soil falls apart.

flow.context: In this step you make a ribbon from each soil, to feel how much clay it has.

flow.do: Write what you found in the table. Ask: which of these soils would hold the most water, and which would drain the fastest?
flow.say: Which soil would hold the most water in a pot? Which would let it run through? How can you tell by feel?
flow.kid: Which soil holds water? Which drains?
flow.parent: Clay holds the most water and drains slowest. Sand drains fastest. The garden soil is in between.

activities.title: Takers and Givers: sort twelve crops by what they do to the soil

materials.item: 12 small squares of paper, about the size of a playing card
a pencil
a sheet of paper folded into three columns
a notebook

schedule.what: Write twelve crop cards, sort them by what they do to nitrogen, and plan a rotation.

activities.record: Your three columns of crops, and your four-season plan for one field.

flow.do: Write one crop on each paper square: rice, wheat, maize, sugarcane, cotton, ragi, bajra, moong, urad, chana, groundnut, red gram.
flow.say: Write one crop on each square. Some of these take a lot from the soil. Some give to it. Some ask for little.
flow.kid: Write one crop on each square.
flow.context: This is the first step of Takers and Givers. You make twelve crop cards.

flow.do: Fold a sheet into three columns: Takes a lot of nitrogen, Gives nitrogen, and Needs little. Put each card in the column you think is right. Ask for the reason as you go.
flow.say: Where does each crop go? Which are the legumes? Which are the cereals that grow tall and fast? Which grow even in poor soil?
flow.kid: Sort the cards into three columns. Say why.

ask.q: Which crops put nitrogen into the soil, and how can you tell?
good: Moong, urad, chana, groundnut and red gram.
They have pods.
They are the beans and pulses.

flow.parent: The answers are these. Takes a lot: rice, wheat, maize, sugarcane, cotton. Gives: moong, urad, chana, groundnut, red gram. Needs little: ragi and bajra. Legumes have seeds in pods. The millets are tough crops that grow well in poor, dry soil.

check.q: Which of these crops fixes nitrogen with bacteria in her roots?
options: Wheat
Groundnut
Maize
check.why: Groundnut is a legume, so her roots grow nodules with nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Wheat and maize are cereals, which take a lot of nitrogen from the soil.

flow.context: In this step you sort twelve crops by what they do to the nitrogen in the soil.

flow.do: Plan eight seasons for one field with the cards. Put one crop in each season. Use each pulse at least twice. Never put the same crop in two seasons in a row.
flow.say: Plan a field for eight seasons. A cereal, then a pulse, then a cereal again. How will you keep the soil from getting tired?
flow.kid: Plan eight seasons. Mix cereals and pulses.
flow.parent: Many answers work. One good plan is rice, black gram, rice, groundnut, ragi, red gram, rice, moong. Ask your child why the pulses are placed where they are. With two to four children, each plans a field alone, then swaps with a neighbour, who checks the two rules and finds the first season that might fail.
flow.think: What would happen to the soil after eight seasons of only rice?
