activities.title: Nodule Hunt: find the pink pearls on a bean's roots (if you can get a whole plant)

materials.item: a whole legume plant with roots: a groundnut plant (sold in some vegetable markets after harvest, ask the seller to keep the roots), or a chana, pea or cowpea plant dug up with a spade from a garden or field (ask a farmer or neighbour), or a moong plant you grew in garden soil for 4 to 5 weeks. Dig the whole root with soil around it, do not pull
a bowl of water
a magnifying glass, if you have one
a small sharp knife or a new blade, for a grown-up to use (or just squeeze a nodule between two fingernails)
a white plate

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the nodules, because the knife is sharp. Groundnut is a common allergen: if anyone in the family is allergic to peanuts, use a moong or pea plant instead. Wash hands after touching the roots and the soil.

schedule.what: Wash the roots, find the nodules, cut one open and look at the colour inside.

activities.record: Draw the roots with the nodules on them. Draw one cut nodule and colour the inside.

flow.do: Hold the plant over the bowl. Wash the soil off the roots very gently, by dipping them and swirling them in water. Do not pull.
flow.say: Wash the roots gently. Dip, swirl, and look. Do not pull, because the nodules can break off.
flow.kid: Dip the roots in water. Wash gently. Do not pull.
flow.context: This is a hunt for root nodules on a bean plant. You wash the soil off the roots first.
flow.parent: Soak the soil clump in water for a few minutes first, so the soil falls off by itself. Nodules rub off easily, so swirl, do not scrub. With two to four children, share one plant: each child counts the nodules on a different root and everyone adds up.

flow.do: Look at the roots on a white plate. Find the small round bumps stuck to the roots. Count how many you can find. Find a bump on a thin side root.
flow.say: Look for round bumps on the roots. They are the nodules. How many can you count? How big is the biggest?
flow.kid: Look for round bumps on the roots. Count them.

ask.q: What do the bumps look like?
good: Little round beads.
Small and round, like a sesame seed.
Smooth and stuck to the root.

flow.parent: Nodules on groundnut are small, round and a little pale or brown on the outside, from about 1 to 5 millimetres across. If you find none, the plant may have grown in soil without the right bacteria, or the roots may have been trimmed. That is real, and worth writing down. Nodules rub off with a finger; swollen lumps that are part of the root and will not rub off are not nodules (they may be galls made by tiny worms). A plant from a market after harvest is at the end of its life, so its nodules may be few and old.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts one big nodule in half with the knife. Look at the cut surface inside with the magnifying glass. What colour is it?
flow.say: A grown-up cuts a nodule in half. What colour is the inside? Pink means the nodule is working.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts a nodule open. What colour is the inside?
flow.parent: A pink or reddish inside means the nodule is working and fixing nitrogen. A white or green inside means it has stopped. The pink comes from a substance that holds oxygen back from the nitrogen-fixing tool. Dried or old nodules look brown or green inside. On a plant sold after harvest this is common, so do not be surprised if none is pink: write down what you see, and try a younger plant (chana or moong at flowering time) if you can. Pink is clearest in nodules cut from a living, flowering plant.

check.q: A cut nodule is bright pink inside. What does this tell you?
options: The nodule is working and fixing nitrogen
The nodule is full of juice
The nodule is rotting
check.why: The pink comes from a substance the nodule makes to hold oxygen back from the nitrogen-fixing tool. A white or green nodule is no longer working.

flow.context: In this step you cut open a nodule to see if it is working.

flow.do: Look at the root of a grass or a cereal, such as a weed from a pot. Does it have nodules?
flow.say: Compare with a root from a grass. Does it have the same round bumps?
flow.kid: Look at a grass root. Does it have bumps?
flow.parent: Grasses and cereals have no nodules. They take their nitrogen from the soil.

activities.context: In this activity you look for the nodules on the roots of a legume, and cut one open to see if it is working.

activities.title: Soil Doctor: read a field's soil card and write a plan

materials.item: a pencil and a notebook
a made-up soil card, which is written out in step 1 of this activity

schedule.what: Read a made-up soil card. Decide what the field needs. Write a plan for the farmer.

activities.record: A plan for the field in three sentences: what the card says, what the field needs and what the farmer should do.

flow.do: Read this made-up card for a field near Thanjavur. Nitrogen is low. Phosphorus is medium. Potassium is high. Acidity is 8.1, which is slightly alkaline. Salt is low. Humus is low.
flow.say: This is a card for a farmer's field. Nitrogen is low. Phosphorus is medium. Potassium is high. The soil is slightly alkaline. Salt is low. Humus is low.
flow.kid: Read the card. What is low? What is high?

ask.q: Which parts of the card are not good for a crop?
good: Nitrogen is low.
Humus is low.
The others are fine.

flow.parent: The card is made up. A real Soil Health Card from the Government of India lists the same kinds of things for a real field. A farmer gets one free every two years or so.
flow.context: This is the first step of Soil Doctor. You read a soil card, as a farmer would, and decide what the field needs.

flow.do: Write what the field needs. Choose from these: grow a pulse, add compost or manure, add urea, leave the field fallow, do nothing. Choose two things and say why.
flow.say: Which two things would you do for this field? Why? What does each one fix?
flow.kid: Choose two things for the field. Say why.
flow.parent: Good answers: grow a pulse to add nitrogen and add compost to raise the humus. Adding some urea is also reasonable for a quick boost of nitrogen. Leaving the field fallow does not add nitrogen. Adding nothing is not wise, because nitrogen and humus are both low. With two to four children, each picks two things alone, then the group argues for the best pair.

check.q: The card says nitrogen is low and humus is low. Which two things help most?
options: Grow a pulse and add compost
Add salt and grow rice again
Leave the field bare and do nothing
check.why: A pulse brings nitrogen into the soil, and compost adds humus. Salt would harm the crop, and doing nothing leaves both problems.

flow.context: In this step you choose what the field needs.

flow.do: Write your plan in three sentences for the farmer. Say what the card says, what the field needs and what to do.
flow.say: Write three sentences for the farmer. What does the card say? What does the field need? What should she do?
flow.kid: Write three sentences for the farmer.
flow.think: How would the farmer know in two years whether the plan worked?

activities.context: In this activity you read a made-up soil card for a field and write a plan for the farmer.

activities.title: Crack Maker: why does clay crack when it dries?

materials.item: two small plates (plastic or steel, not your best crockery)
a few tablespoons of multani mitti (Fuller's earth), or wet clay
a few tablespoons of clean sand
water and a spoon
a ruler

activities.safety: Wash hands after touching the clay, in a bowl, not the sink, because clay can block drains. Do not put clay in your mouth.

schedule.what: Make two pastes, spread them on plates and put them in the Sun.
Look at the cracks and measure them.

activities.record: Draw both plates. Write which one cracked, and the width of the widest crack.

flow.do: Mix 4 tablespoons of multani mitti with water to make a thick paste. Mix 2 tablespoons of multani mitti, 2 tablespoons of sand and water to make a second paste.
flow.say: Plate A is all clay. Plate B is half clay and half sand. Which will crack more when it dries? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Make two pastes. One is all clay. One is half sand.

ask.q: Which plate do you think will crack more, and why?
good: The clay one, because it holds more water.
The sandy one, because it is rough.
Neither will crack.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Crack Maker. You make two pastes to find out which one cracks as it dries.

flow.do: Spread each paste about 5 millimetres thick on its own plate. Put both plates in the same sunny place.
flow.say: Spread both pastes to the same thickness. Put them side by side in the Sun.
flow.kid: Spread both pastes. Put them in the sun.

flow.do: Look at both plates. Measure the widest crack in each with a ruler. Draw what you see.
flow.say: Look at the plates. Which one cracked? How wide is the widest crack?
flow.kid: Look at both plates. Which one cracked?
flow.parent: The all-clay plate usually cracks into pieces with wide gaps. The sandy plate usually cracks much less, or not at all. If both crack alike, write that down. The cracking is stronger when the paste is thick and dries fast. Multani mitti paste in strong sun usually cracks in a few hours. In a damp or cloudy spell it can take two or three days: leave it longer and keep the plates in the same place. One child with a parent: make the two plates. Two to four children: each child makes a plate with a different mix (all clay, three clay to one sand, one clay to one sand, one clay to three sand) and you line the plates up from most to least cracked.

check.q: The all-clay plate cracked and the sandy plate hardly did. What is the best reason?
options: Clay holds a lot of water and shrinks a lot as it dries
Sand is heavier than clay
Clay is hotter than sand
check.why: Clay grains are tiny and hold a lot of water between them. As the water leaves, the clay shrinks, and the shrinking pulls it apart into cracks. Sand holds little water and hardly shrinks.

flow.context: In this step you look at the two plates after one day.

activities.context: In this activity you dry a clay paste and a clay-and-sand paste in the Sun, to see why the black soil of the Deccan cracks in summer.

setup.caption: 1. Spread both pastes and put them in the sun.

setup.art: The same two plates a day later, the clay plate split into pieces with wide gaps and the sandy plate with only fine lines.
setup.caption: 2. Look at the cracks next day.

activities.title: Cabbage Water Test: is the soil acid or alkaline?

materials.item: a few leaves of red cabbage (sold in bigger vegetable shops and supermarkets; no red cabbage? see the note in step 1)
hot water from a kettle or pan, in a heatproof bowl
seven clear glasses, a jug and a bowl
white vinegar (or lemon juice), baking soda
two spoons of garden soil and a pinch of wood ash from a chulha (or two spoons of crushed school chalk)
a spoon and a sieve or tea strainer

activities.safety: A grown-up heats the water and pours it. The water is hot. Do not taste the cabbage water, the vinegar, the baking soda, the ash or the chalk, and do not breathe in the ash or chalk dust. Keep the vinegar, baking soda and ash away from eyes. Wash hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Make cabbage water. Test vinegar and baking soda. Then test soil water and ash water.

activities.record: A table of five glasses with the colour of each: plain, vinegar, baking soda, soil water and ash (or chalk) water.

flow.do: A grown-up pours hot water over torn red cabbage leaves in a bowl and waits for 10 minutes. Strain it into a jug. The purple liquid is your test liquid.
flow.say: Soak the cabbage leaves in hot water. The water turns purple. This is our test liquid.
flow.kid: A grown-up soaks cabbage in hot water. It turns purple.
flow.parent: Let the water cool before children touch it. The liquid turns pink with acid and blue-green with alkali. No red cabbage? Stir a teaspoon of turmeric powder into half a glass of water: it stays yellow with vinegar and turns red-brown with baking soda. The colours are less clear than cabbage, but it works. With two to four children, each child tests one glass and says the colour before the others look.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cabbage Water Test. You make a purple liquid that changes colour with acid and alkali.

flow.do: Pour the same amount of purple liquid into three glasses. Add a spoon of vinegar to one. Add half a spoon of baking soda to another. Leave the third plain. Look at the colours.
flow.say: Vinegar is acid. Baking soda is alkaline. What colour does each make? What does the plain glass look like?
flow.kid: Add vinegar to one glass. Add baking soda to another. Look at the colours.

ask.q: What colour did the vinegar make, and what colour did the baking soda make?
good: Pink for the vinegar.
Green or blue for the baking soda.
The plain one stays purple.

flow.parent: Vinegar turns the liquid pink or red. Baking soda turns it blue-green. Plain is purple. These are your colour guide.

flow.do: Stir a spoon of garden soil into a glass of water. Stir a spoon of wood ash (or chalk powder) into another glass of water. Let both settle for 5 minutes. Pour the clear water on top into two fresh glasses of purple liquid. Compare the colours.
flow.say: Which colour does the soil water make? Which does the ash or chalk water make? Compare them with your guide.
flow.kid: Test the soil water and the ash water. Compare the colours.
flow.parent: Garden soil water usually stays close to purple, and may lean a little pink or blue. Ash water turns the liquid green or blue-green, because wood ash is alkaline. Some school chalk is gypsum, which is nearly neutral, so chalk water may show little change: if so, say so, and use ash. A soil that fizzes with vinegar has chalk in it. If your soil water changes colour a little, say which side it leans towards.

check.q: The ash water turns the purple liquid blue-green. What does this tell you?
options: Ash is alkaline
Ash is acidic
Ash has no effect
check.why: Blue-green is the colour the purple liquid turns in an alkaline liquid, like baking soda. Many chalky soils and ash are alkaline too.

flow.context: In this step you test soil water and chalk water with the purple liquid.

activities.context: In this activity you make a purple liquid from red cabbage that changes colour with acid and alkali, and use it to test soil.

projects.title: Bean Before Methi: does a pot that grew moong feed the next crop?

materials.item: two pots of the same size, about 20 centimetres wide, with holes in the bottom (or two ice-cream tubs with holes)
poor soil: half garden soil from a place where beans have grown and half washed sand. No garden? Use soil from a pot that held a bean or pulse.
about 12 whole green moong seeds and about 20 methi seeds, from the kirana (food seeds, not coloured treated packet seeds)
a bowl, a ruler, scissors and a notebook
a sunny window or balcony

schedule.what: Fill two pots with the same poor soil. Sow 6 moong seeds in pot A. Leave pot B bare. Water both.
Pull up one moong plant from pot A and look for nodules. Cut the other plants at soil level and leave the roots.
Sow 10 methi seeds in each pot.
Count and measure the methi in each pot.
Measure again, compare the pots and write your result.

projects.record: A table with the pot, the number of methi seedlings, the height of the tallest and the leaf colour on days 36 and 43. Draw the two pots on day 43.

flow.do: Fill both pots with the same poor soil. In pot A, sow 6 moong seeds about 2 centimetres deep. Leave pot B with no seeds. Water both with the same amount, and put them side by side.
flow.say: Both pots have the same poor soil. Pot A grows moong. Pot B stays bare. Later we will grow methi in both. Which pot will grow better methi? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two pots, same soil. Moong in A. Nothing in B. Water both.

ask.q: Why do you think one pot might grow better methi than the other?
good: The moong roots left something in the soil.
The moong gave nitrogen.
Both pots will be the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Use soil that has had beans or pulses grown in it, so the right bacteria are in the soil. Poor soil makes any difference easier to see. One child with a parent: one pair of pots. Two to four children: each child grows their own pair, and you pool the results at the end. If most pairs go the same way the result is more believable.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bean Before Methi, a six-week project. You grow moong in one pot, then methi in both, to see if the moong changes the soil.

flow.do: Water both pots the same amount every day or two, so the soil stays slightly damp (every day in hot weather). Pull weeds out of both pots. On day 21, pull up one moong plant from pot A. Wash the roots in a bowl. Look for nodules. Cut the rest of the moong at soil level and leave the roots in the pot.
flow.say: After three weeks, pull up one moong plant. Look for round bumps on her roots. Cut the others at the soil and leave the roots in.
flow.kid: Pull up one moong plant. Look for round bumps. Cut the rest at the soil.

ask.q: What do you see on the roots?
good: Small round bumps.
No bumps at all.
Tiny white beads.

flow.parent: If you see nodules, cut one open to see the pink colour. If you see none, the soil may not hold the right bacteria. Carry on with the project, and write down that there were none.
flow.wait: Leave the pots a day, then sow methi on day 22.

flow.do: On day 22, sow 10 methi seeds in each pot, about 1 centimetre deep. Water both pots the same amount. Keep them side by side in the sun.
flow.say: Now sow methi in both pots. Same seeds, same water, same sun. Only the pot's history is different.
flow.kid: Sow 10 methi seeds in each pot. Water the same.
flow.wait: Water both pots every day or two. Look again on day 36.

flow.do: On day 36, count the seedlings in each pot. Measure the tallest seedling in each. Look at the colour of the leaves. Write all of this in the table.
flow.say: Count the methi in each pot. Measure the tallest. Which leaves are greener?
flow.kid: Count the methi. Measure the tallest. Look at the colour.
flow.parent: If the pots look alike, write that down: it is a real result. The effect of one bean crop can be small. Green leaves mean more nitrogen. Pale yellow-green leaves often mean too little. The pots may differ by only a little, or the bare pot may even look better. That can happen if the moong used up the nitrogen before it was cut. Write down what you see.
flow.wait: Water both pots every day or two. Look again on day 43.

flow.do: On day 43, measure again. Compare the pots. Ask your child for the three things: what I think, what I saw and why.
flow.say: What is different between the pots now? What do you think the moong did? How could we be sure?
flow.kid: What is different now? What did the moong do?
flow.parent: Be honest with your child. Two pots are a small test, and many things can differ. A strong test uses many pots. Ask what she would change to be surer.

check.q: Methi in the pot that grew moong stands taller and greener. What is the best explanation?
options: Bacteria in the moong roots added nitrogen to the soil
Methi likes the smell of moong
The moong plants kept the Sun off
check.why: Moong roots carry nitrogen-fixing bacteria, and the roots left in the pot add nitrogen as they rot. Methi leaves use nitrogen to grow green. Other differences between the pots can also matter, so this is a hint, and not a proof.

projects.context: In this project you grow moong in one pot and leave another bare, then grow methi in both. You find out whether a pot that grew a bean feeds the next crop.

challenges.title: Wick the Pot: water a plant for three days without pouring
challenges.problem: A family will be away for three days. Design a way to keep a potted plant's soil damp for three days with one 500 millilitre bottle of water, and without anyone pouring water on the soil.
constraints: Use one bottle that holds 500 millilitres of water. Fill it once at the start.
Nobody may pour water on the soil for three days.
Use only things from home, such as cotton rope, strips of old cloth and a bucket.
Check the soil with a clean pencil pushed 5 centimetres into the soil. Wet, dark soil sticks to the pencil.
Use the same kind of pot, soil and plant for every design.
materials: a potted plant or a pot of damp soil
strips of old cotton cloth or thick cotton rope
general: Stand the bottle next to the pot. Run a cotton wick from the water to the soil. The water climbs the wick, just as it climbed the cup of sand.
Stand the pot on a plate of water, with a wick from the plate through the hole in the bottom of the pot.
Water the pot very well before you leave, then lay a thick cover of dry leaves on the soil.
creative: Bury a small unglazed clay pot in the soil and fill it with water. The water slowly seeps through the clay into the soil. This is called pitcher irrigation, and farmers use it in dry places.
Use two wicks from two sides, to spread the water.
Hang the bottle upside down with a wick running out of the cap.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own way. Draw it first. Build it and fill the bottle. Check the soil with the pencil each day. Which design kept the soil damp for three days, and why?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the materials. Ask your child to draw two or three different designs.
flow.say: A plant must drink for three days, with no one pouring. What have we learned about how water moves? How can we use it?
flow.kid: Draw two or three ways to water the pot without pouring.

ask.q: What helped the water to climb in the sand cup?
good: The tiny gaps between the grains.
The gaps in the cloth.
Water sticking to the grains.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Wick the Pot challenge. You plan a way to keep a pot damp by using what you know about how water climbs.

flow.do: Build your first design. Fill the bottle. Water the soil well at the start. Push a pencil 5 centimetres into the soil and write down how it looks.
flow.say: Build your idea. Fill the bottle. Test the soil with the pencil. Write down what you see.
flow.kid: Build your design. Test the soil with the pencil.
flow.parent: Soak the wick before you put it in. A dry wick is slow to start. Stand the bottle higher than the soil, so the water has a short way to climb. Do not put the wick in with a tight loop, because a kink can block the water.
flow.context: In this step you build your first design.

flow.do: On days 2 and 3, push the pencil into the soil again and write down how it looks. Look at the level of water in the bottle.
flow.say: Check the soil each day. Is it still damp? How much water is left in the bottle?
flow.kid: Check the soil each day. Is it still damp?
flow.parent: A long wick is slow. A short, thick wick moves more water. Check the pencil, and the water level in the bottle.
flow.wait: Check again on day 2 and day 3.

flow.do: Choose the design that kept the soil damp best. Ask why. Change one thing and test again, if you have time.
flow.say: Which design worked best? Why? What would you change to make it better?
flow.kid: Which design worked best? Why? What would you change?
flow.think: How could a wick tell when the plant has had enough?

check.q: Your wick pulled water from the bottle into the soil. What lifted the water?
options: Water sticking to the threads of the cloth and pulling the water behind it
The wick pumped the water
The soil sucked the water
check.why: The wick works like the cup of sand. Water sticks to the fine threads, and pulls on the water behind it, so it climbs. Nothing pumps it and nothing sucks it.

challenges.context: This is a design challenge about capillary rise. You use what you know about how water climbs to keep a pot damp for three days.

challenges.title: The Four-Year Plan: plan a field that never runs out of nitrogen
challenges.problem: A family has one small field and grows two crops a year, so eight seasons in four years. Plan the eight crops so that the nitrogen bank never runs empty, the family has rice at least four times, and there is a pulse in at least three seasons.
constraints: Use the crop cards from the game Soil Bank, or write your own, with the same costs and gains.
Start with a bank of 4 nitrogen tokens.
At the end of every season, add 1 token for rain, leaves and the bacteria in the soil.
The bank must never fall below 0, and you may not grow the same crop in two seasons in a row.
Write the bank at the end of each season in your plan.
materials: the crop cards from Soil Bank
a sheet of paper with eight rows for the eight seasons
nitrogen tokens, dried beans or buttons
general: Rice, then black gram, then rice, then groundnut, and so on, like the rice and pulse pattern in the Kaveri delta.
Two cereals, then a pulse, then a rest, so the bank has time to fill.
Ragi in some seasons, because it asks little of the soil.
creative: Grow ragi with a row of red gram between, and count the red gram as a pulse in the same season.
Grow azolla in the rice field to feed the rice with nitrogen, and count it as a gift of 1 token.
Leave one season fallow, and plant a cover crop of any plant so the soil is not bare.
challenges.your_turn: Now plan your own four years. Write each season's crop and the nitrogen bank. Check it with your tokens. Swap your plan with someone else and see if it works for them. Which plan earned the most points?

flow.do: Read the problem. Write down the numbers: the bank starts at 4, and every season ends with 1 token added.
flow.say: Our bank starts at 4. Every season adds 1 token at the end. Rice takes 3. How low will the bank be after two rice seasons?
flow.kid: The bank starts at 4. Rice takes 3. Work out two rice seasons.

ask.q: What happens to the bank if you grow rice two seasons in a row?
good: It falls to about 1 or 0.
The next rice fails.
You must put a pulse in.

flow.parent: Rice, then rice: 4 minus 3 is 1, plus 1 is 2. Then 2 is not enough for 3, so the crop fails. The rule says never to grow the same crop twice in a row, but the sums show why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Four-Year Plan challenge. You plan eight crops for a field and keep track of its nitrogen.

flow.do: Write your first plan of eight crops. Work out the bank after every season. Cross out any plan where the bank would go below 0.
flow.say: Plan the eight seasons. Work out the bank after each. If it goes below 0, change the plan.
flow.kid: Plan eight seasons. Work out the bank each time.
flow.parent: A good plan follows a heavy crop with a pulse. Pulses give 2 tokens, plus 1 at the end of the season, so they raise the bank by 3.

flow.do: Swap plans with a second player. Check each other's sums. Find the plan with the most points. Talk about what each plan costs and gains.
flow.say: Check someone else's plan. Does the bank stay above 0? Which plan earns more?
flow.kid: Swap plans. Check the sums. Which earns more?
flow.think: Why would a real farmer's plan be harder than this game?

check.q: A plan grows rice, then moong, then rice, then moong. The bank starts at 4. What is the bank after four seasons?
check.why: Season 1: rice takes 3, so the bank is 1, and plus 1 makes 2. Season 2: moong gives 2, so 4, and plus 1 makes 5. Season 3: rice takes 3, so 2, and plus 1 makes 3. Season 4: moong gives 2, so 5, and plus 1 makes 6. The bank after four seasons is 6.

items.p: Which of these soils holds the most water and drains the slowest?
items.why: Clay has the finest grains, so it has the most grain surface for water to cling to and the tiniest gaps. Water drains from it very slowly. Sand and gravel have big gaps and let water run through.

items.p: Water climbing up through the narrow gaps in soil is called capillary ____.
items.why: Capillary rise is the climb of water through very narrow gaps against gravity, as in a wick or a cloth.

items.p: Water climbed about 1 centimetre in a cup of gravel and nearly to the top of a cup of sand. Why did gravel lift the water so little?
opts: The gaps in gravel are too wide to pull the water up far
items.why: Water is lifted by its stickiness to the grains at the edge of a gap. In very wide gaps most of the water is far from any grain, so the pull is weak. Weight is not what matters.

items.p: A cover of dry leaves on top of a pot makes the soil under it lose water faster.
items.why: False. The leaves shade the soil and block the wind, so less water evaporates. That is why farmers spread straw as mulch.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: Loam
a soil with some sand, silt, clay and humus
Mulch
a cover of straw or leaves laid on soil
Legume
a plant from the bean family
Fallow
a field left to rest for a season
Nodule
a swelling on a root where helper bacteria live
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These five words are used all through the unit.

items.p: Sort these crops by what they do to the nitrogen in a field.
items.a: see items
items.why: Rice, wheat and maize are cereals that need a lot of nitrogen. Groundnut, moong and chana are legumes with nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their roots.

items.p: A pot of pure sand needs watering much more often than a pot of garden soil. Explain why, using what you know about grains and gaps.
items.a: Sand has big grains with big gaps, and the water runs straight through. Little clings to the grains. Garden soil has finer grains and humus, which hold water in thin films and in the gaps.
items.why: A strong answer links the size of the grains and gaps to how much water is held and how fast it drains.

items.p: A rice field has pale yellow leaves. Which nutrient is it most likely short of?
items.why: Nitrogen builds leaf proteins and chlorophyll, so a shortage gives pale yellow leaves. Salt is not a nutrient plants need in large amounts, and sand is not a nutrient.

items.p: Label this drawing of a bean root: main root, nodule, soil, arrow of nitrogen from the air, arrow of sugar from the leaf.
items.a: The main root runs down through the soil. Round nodules sit on the side roots. An arrow of nitrogen runs from the air through the soil to the nodule. An arrow of sugar runs from the leaf down to the nodule.
items.why: The nodule is where the two arrows meet. The bacteria receive sugar and give nitrogen.
items.art: An unlabelled bean plant with roots in soil, round nodules on the roots, a dotted arrow from the air to a nodule and another dotted arrow from a leaf to the same nodule.

items.p: Urea has 46 per cent nitrogen, so 100 kilograms of urea holds ____ kilograms of nitrogen.
items.why: 46 per cent means 46 parts in every 100. In 100 kilograms of urea, 46 kilograms is nitrogen.

items.p: Draw your Salty Seeds test on day 3. Show the four saucers and how many seeds sprouted in each.
items.a: Four saucers in a row. The plain saucer has the most sprouted seeds, the pinch of salt saucer has a few less, the half spoon saucer has very few and the one spoon saucer has none.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the number of sprouts falling as the salt rises.
items.art: A page with four empty circles for saucers and a column for notes.

items.p: A white crust of salt forms on the top of a dry field that has been watered for many years. Where did the salt come from?
opts: It was in the irrigation water, and stayed behind when the water evaporated
It rose from the sky in the rain
It was made by the roots of the crop
items.why: All irrigation water carries a little dissolved salt. When the water evaporates or is used by plants, the salt stays behind and builds up.

items.p: Moong, urad, chana and groundnut are all legumes.
items.why: True. They all belong to the bean family and have seeds in pods. Their roots carry nodules with nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

items.p: A gardener lays dry leaves on the soil of a pot and the soil stays damp for twice as long. Say why.
items.a: The leaves shade the soil and stop the wind from reaching it. So less water turns into vapour and leaves the soil. The water stays in the pot for longer.
items.why: A strong answer says that mulch cuts the evaporation from the top.

items.p: Put these steps in order, from the air to the bean.
items: Nitrogen gas is in the air
Bacteria in a nodule change the gas into ammonia
The bean plant turns the ammonia into protein
The bean seed is full of protein
A family eats the bean as dal
a: Nitrogen gas is in the air
Bacteria in a nodule change the gas into ammonia
The bean plant turns the ammonia into protein
The bean seed is full of protein
A family eats the bean as dal
items.why: Nitrogen gas is turned into ammonia by the bacteria, the plant builds it into protein, and the protein ends in the seed. We eat the seed.

items.p: What does a bean plant give the bacteria in her nodules?
items.why: The bean makes sugar in her leaves with the help of sunlight, and gives some to the bacteria. The bacteria give nitrogen in return.

items.p: Two cups of soil are poured with 100 millilitres of water. The first holds back 80 millilitres. The second holds back 30. Which soil has more clay?
items.why: Clay holds a lot of water in its tiny gaps and drains slowly. The soil that holds back more water is likely to have more clay.

items.p: Fine soil took longer than sand to wet, but in time it could lift water higher. Explain both parts.
items.a: Water is pulled up by its stickiness to the grains. In fine soil the gaps are narrower, so the pull is stronger and the water can rise higher in the end. But narrow gaps are harder for water to flow through, so the climb is slower.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason for the higher climb and a reason for the slower climb.

items.p: Sand is wet to the top of a cup in 20 minutes, and fine soil is wet only 2 centimetres up. What will fine soil do if you wait a few more days?
opts: It will stay at 2 centimetres for ever
It will keep climbing, slowly, and may go much higher
items.why: Fine soil lifts water higher in the end than sand does, but takes much longer. So it keeps climbing slowly.

items.p: A gardener and a farmer disagree about the dry season.

views.says: Cover the soil in dry leaves. It keeps the water in.
Hoe the top of the soil. It breaks the paths the water climbs.
Both help in some soils. Mulch works best in most tests, but you can try both.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Use what you know about capillary rise and evaporation. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and gives a reason from the unit, such as shading the soil or breaking the narrow paths, and admits a fair point from another view.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Scientists find that mulch works well in most tests and that hoeing helps in some soils, so a fair answer weighs both.

items.p: Fertiliser is food for plants.
items.why: False. Plants make their own food from air, water and light. Fertiliser gives the nutrients they need to build their bodies, like the bricks, and not the meal.

items.p: About four fifths of the air is ____ gas.
items.why: Air is about 78 parts nitrogen in every 100. Plants cannot use it as a gas.

items.p: A nodule has a red-pink substance inside. What does it do?
opts: It holds back oxygen, which would damage the nitrogen-fixing tool
items.why: The tool the bacteria use to break the nitrogen bond is harmed by oxygen. The pink substance holds oxygen back so the tool keeps working.

items.p: Sort these actions by what they do to the water in the soil of a field.
items: leaving bare soil in the hot Sun
watering the roots with a slow drip
flooding the whole field when only the roots need it
covering the soil with a plastic sheet
items.a: see items
items.why: Covers slow evaporation and shade the soil. Drip watering wets only the roots. Bare soil in the Sun and flooding let more water go to the air or drain away.

items.p: A shopkeeper says that soil is like a bank. Crops empty it, and only fertiliser can fill it. Use what you know about beans to say what is missing from that picture.
items.a: A bean crop can put nitrogen into the soil, with bacteria in her roots. Rotting roots and leaves, manure and rain also add nutrients. So soil is not only emptied and filled by people. Living things fill it too.
items.why: A strong answer names the bacteria and the roots, and says that living things add nitrogen.

items.p: A farmer grows wheat in the same field year after year. What problem can build up?
opts: Pests and diseases that attack wheat can build up, and the soil's nitrogen can run low
The field turns into a pond
items.why: A pest that feeds on wheat finds food every year if wheat is always there. Wheat also takes a lot of nitrogen, with nothing putting it back. A rotation breaks both problems.

items.p: Draw a field with a white salt crust on top. Show where the water came from, where it went and where the salt stayed.
items.a: An irrigation channel on one side bringing water. Water vapour rising from the field into the air. A white crust of salt on the soil. A drain at the far end carrying away some salt.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the water leaves as vapour and the salt stays behind.
items.art: A field outline with an irrigation channel on the left and a drain on the right.

items.p: Match each place or plant to what it shows about soil.
pairs: Pokkali rice in Kerala
a crop that copes with salty water
Tea in the Nilgiris
a crop that likes acid soil
Azolla in a paddy
a fern that carries nitrogen-fixing bacteria
Ragi with red gram
an example of growing crops together
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of these shows how a plant or a farmer works with the soil.

items.p: Which field is most likely to get a white salt crust?
opts: A dry field watered from a canal for many years
A forest floor that gets heavy rain every year
A field that has just been ploughed
items.why: Where rain is heavy it washes salt away. In a dry place, irrigation water evaporates and leaves its salt behind, year after year.

items.p: Put these in order to show how salt builds up in a dry irrigated field.
items: Canal water carrying a little salt is spread on the field
The Sun and the crop use up the water
The salt stays in the soil
Year after year, the salt builds up
A white crust forms on the top of the soil
a: Canal water carrying a little salt is spread on the field
The Sun and the crop use up the water
The salt stays in the soil
Year after year, the salt builds up
A white crust forms on the top of the soil
items.why: Only the water leaves. The salt stays and adds up over the years.

items.p: A soil card says the nitrogen is low and the potassium is high. What would you tell the farmer?
items.a: Grow a pulse in the field, add compost or manure, and perhaps some urea. The potassium is high, so she does not need to add more.
items.why: A strong answer matches the advice to what is low and leaves out what is high.

items.p: If the whole bean plant is taken from the field at harvest, the soil may gain little nitrogen.
items.why: True. A lot of the nitrogen goes into the seeds and the leaves. If these are all taken away, little returns to the soil. The gain is greatest when the roots and leaves are left to rot in the field.

items.p: On the pH scale, a pH of 7 means the soil is ____.
items.why: Seven is neutral. Lower numbers are acidic and higher numbers are alkaline.

items.p: Water climbs 5 centimetres in one soil in 10 minutes, then stops. In a second soil it climbs 2 centimetres in 10 minutes, and keeps rising for hours. Which soil has the finer gaps?
items.why: Finer gaps pull harder, so water can keep rising, but they flow slowly. The soil that climbs slowly and keeps going has the finer gaps.

items.p: A cotton wick from a bottle to a pot waters a plant with nothing pushing it. Explain why the water climbs, and why a thick wick moves more water than a thin one.
items.a: Water sticks to the fine threads and pulls the water behind it. A thick wick has more threads and more gaps, so more water moves at once.
items.why: A strong answer names the stickiness between water and the threads, and says that more threads carry more water.

items.p: A 50 kilogram bag of urea has 46 per cent nitrogen. It holds ____ kilograms of nitrogen.
items.why: 46 per cent of 50 is half of 46, which is 23.

items.p: A town is deciding how to feed its kitchen gardens.

views.who: Meena, a gardener who uses only compost
views.says: Compost feeds the soil life and adds humus. Factory fertiliser can wash into rivers.

views.who: Joseph, a farmer who uses fertiliser
views.says: My crops need a lot of nitrogen fast. Compost is not enough for a big harvest.
Use both. Compost builds the soil, and a little fertiliser fills the gap.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from the unit. Then say what another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view with a reason, such as soil life and humus, or the need for nitrogen, and says what a different view gets right.
items.why: Organic and chemical farming is a real argument. Plants take up the same nitrate ions from both, but compost also builds the soil, so many scientists suggest using both.

items.p: Growing a pulse always leaves more nitrogen in the soil than there was before.
items.why: False. The gain depends on what happens to the plants. If the beans and the plants are taken away, the soil may gain little or lose nitrogen.

items.p: Label the cut nodule: root, nodule wall, pink centre with bacteria, nitrogen arriving, sugar arriving.
items.a: The nodule sits on the root. Its pink centre is full of bacteria. Nitrogen gas arrives from the soil air and sugar arrives from the plant.
items.why: The pink substance holds oxygen back so the nitrogen-fixing tool is safe.
items.art: An unlabelled cross-section of a root with a round nodule and a pink centre, with four blank label lines.

items.p: Pokkali rice can grow in salty water. Give one idea for how a plant might cope with salt, and say whether you are sure.
items.a: A plant might keep the salt out of her roots, or store it in old leaves, or make her cells hold water tightly. I am not sure which Pokkali does. Scientists are still studying it.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reasoned idea and says honestly what is not known.

items.p: Draw a hill farm that saves both soil and water. Show at least three things the farmer does.
items.a: Terraces or bunds across the slope, mulch between the rows, plants whose roots hold the soil, and a pond or tank at the bottom to catch the runoff.
items.why: A strong drawing includes things that slow the water, cover the soil and keep the soil.
items.art: A hill outline with a flat valley at the bottom and a small pond.

items.p: Sort these statements by how sure scientists are.
items: Legumes carry bacteria that fix nitrogen
A bean plant punishes nodules that give her little nitrogen
Loosening soil with a hoe always saves water
items.a: see items
items.why: The first, second and last have been measured again and again. The other two depend on the soil, the crop and how the evidence is read.

items.p: The air around a field is full of nitrogen. Why do plants still need fertiliser or bacteria to get nitrogen?
opts: The two atoms in each nitrogen molecule are held together very strongly, and plants cannot break the bond
Nitrogen is too heavy for roots
items.why: Only bacteria with a special tool, or a factory using great heat and pressure, can break that bond.

items.p: Match each person to what they found.
pairs: Hermann Hellriegel and Hermann Wilfarth
peas starved in sand without help from soil bacteria
Martinus Beijerinck
grew the bacteria from the root nodules
Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch
made ammonia from nitrogen gas in a factory
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These three steps moved the story from farmers' habit, to the bacteria, to the factory.

items.p: Your dal is made of protein that holds nitrogen atoms. Write the journey of one nitrogen atom from the air to your body.
items.a: The atom was in nitrogen gas in the air. Bacteria in a nodule changed it into ammonia. The bean plant built it into protein in her seed. A family cooked the seed as dal, and the atom became part of a body.
items.why: Any clear journey is good. A strong answer names the bacteria, the plant and the dal in the right order.

items.p: A farmer wants to lower the amount of fertiliser she buys. Which change helps most?
opts: Grow a pulse in rotation and leave her roots and leaves in the field
Leave the soil bare in the Sun
items.why: A pulse brings nitrogen into the soil through the bacteria in her roots. Leaving the roots and leaves in the field returns the nitrogen to the soil.

items.p: The factory process that makes ammonia from nitrogen gas and hydrogen is named after two German chemists: the ____ process.
items.why: Fritz Haber found the method in 1909 and Carl Bosch made it work in a factory a few years later.

items.p: Some people say that soil is a living thing as a whole. Others say that only the beings in it are alive. What would you want to find out before deciding?
items.a: I would find out whether the soil can grow, take in food, respond and change as a whole, or whether those things are only done by the creatures in it. I would also want to know how much the creatures depend on each other.
items.why: There is no single answer. A strong answer says what evidence would help to decide.

quiz.p: Which soil lets water run through fastest?
quiz.why: Sand has the biggest grains and the biggest gaps, so water runs straight through. Clay holds water in tiny gaps, and loam is in between.

quiz.p: Why do many gardeners like loam?
opts: It drains well and still holds water that roots can use
quiz.why: Loam is a mix of sand, silt, clay and humus. The sand lets extra water out, and the finer grains and humus hold water for roots.

quiz.p: A cup of gravel stood in water. The wet line climbed only about 1 centimetre. What is the best reason?
opts: The gaps are too wide to lift the water far
quiz.why: Water is lifted by its stickiness to the edges of narrow gaps. Wide gaps give a weak pull.

quiz.p: Water moves up through a wick with nobody pushing it. What does the lifting?
opts: Water sticking to the threads and to other water
quiz.why: Water sticks to the surface of the threads, and pulls the water behind it. This is capillary rise.

quiz.p: A bare cup of soil dries more than a cup covered in dry leaves. Why?
opts: The leaves shade the soil and block the wind, so less water evaporates
quiz.why: Evaporation from the top of the soil is slowed by a cover of mulch.

quiz.p: A plant with pale yellow leaves is most likely short of which nutrient?
quiz.why: Nitrogen is needed for leaf proteins and chlorophyll. A plant without enough of it has pale leaves.

quiz.p: The letters N, P and K on a fertiliser bag stand for which nutrients?
quiz.why: The three numbers on the bag give the share of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

quiz.p: Where does the nitrogen in a bean plant's protein first come from?
quiz.why: Bacteria in the nodules take nitrogen gas from the air and change it into ammonia.

quiz.p: What does a bean plant pay the bacteria in her root nodules?
quiz.why: The plant makes sugar in her leaves and gives some to the bacteria. The bacteria give nitrogen back.

quiz.p: A nodule cut in half is bright pink inside. What does this tell you?
opts: The nodule is full of water
quiz.why: The pink substance holds oxygen back so the nitrogen-fixing tool can work. A white or green nodule has stopped.

quiz.p: Why do farmers often follow a cereal with a pulse?
opts: The pulse puts nitrogen back and the next crop does better
quiz.why: A pulse works with bacteria that fix nitrogen, and the roots and leaves left behind add nitrogen. It also breaks the pest cycle of the cereal.

quiz.p: In very salty water, moong seeds did not sprout. What is the best reason?
opts: Salty water holds on to its water so tightly that the seed cannot take it in
Salt makes the seed too heavy
quiz.why: Salty water holds its water tightly, so a seed or root finds it hard to drink. Too much salt also harms the seed.

quiz.p: A dry field watered from a canal for years gets a white crust. What is it?
opts: Salt left behind when the water evaporated
quiz.why: Water carries a little dissolved salt. The water goes into the air and the salt stays.

quiz.p: A soil card says nitrogen is low and humus is low. What is a good plan?
opts: Grow a pulse and add compost
Plough the field and leave it bare
quiz.why: A pulse brings in nitrogen and compost adds humus, so the plan fixes both problems.

open_questions.q: Can rice and wheat be made to grow their own nitrogen-fixing partners?
open_questions.why_open: Researchers are studying maize with sticky root jelly in Mexico and many ways to help cereals host bacteria. Nobody has made it work in a large field yet.

open_questions.q: Does a bean plant choose her bacteria, or does the nodule simply follow how it is built?
open_questions.why_open: Experiments on soybean show nodules that fix less nitrogen do worse, but scientists argue about whether the plant is choosing.

open_questions.q: How much of the water in soil can a root use, and how do roots choose where to take it?
open_questions.why_open: Roots are hidden in the soil and hard to watch. Scientists are still working out how they sense water in the soil and choose where to grow.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of living things live in a handful of soil, and what do they all do?
open_questions.why_open: Most soil bacteria and fungi have never been grown in a laboratory. DNA studies show that there are far more kinds than names.

open_questions.q: How can we feed everyone while using less nitrogen fertiliser, which can wash into rivers?
open_questions.why_open: Better crop rotations, new crops and smarter use of fertiliser all help. How far they can go without lowering harvests is still being tested.

open_questions.q: Why do soil clays hold water so tightly, and could we change that for dry places?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists understand the forces at the surface of clay flakes, but changing soils on a large scale is difficult and slow.

maths.problem: In the Water Climb test, the sand cup was wet to 9 centimetres in 30 minutes. If the water kept climbing at the same speed, how long would it take to reach 12 centimetres? Would it really?
maths.answer: 40 minutes at the same speed, but in real life the climb slows down.
maths.explain: 9 centimetres in 30 minutes is 3 centimetres in 10 minutes. 12 centimetres is 4 lots of 3, so it takes 4 lots of 10 minutes, which is 40 minutes. But the higher the water climbs, the more its own weight pulls it back and the more the gaps slow it, so it takes longer than that.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a distance by a time gives the speed, and a prediction from it shows where the pattern may stop being true.
maths.context: This is about the Water Climb test, where water climbed through a cup of sand.

maths.problem: A bag of urea weighs 50 kilograms. Of every 100 parts, 46 are nitrogen. How many kilograms of nitrogen are in the bag?
maths.explain: 46 per cent of 100 kilograms is 46 kilograms. 50 kilograms is half of 100, so the bag holds half of 46, which is 23 kilograms.
maths.why_maths: Percentages let you work out how much of a bag is the part a farmer pays for.
maths.context: This is about fertiliser bags, which show the share of nitrogen they hold.

maths.problem: In the game Soil Bank, a field starts with 4 tokens. It grows rice (takes 3), then moong (gives 2), then rice again. At the end of each season it gains 1 token. How many tokens are in the bank after three seasons?
maths.explain: Start with 4. Rice takes 3, leaving 1. Add 1 for rain, making 2. Moong gives 2, making 4. Add 1, making 5. Rice takes 3, leaving 2. Add 1, making 3.
maths.why_maths: Adding and subtracting step by step shows how a field's nitrogen changes from one crop to the next.
maths.context: This is about the game Soil Bank, in which crops take nitrogen out of a field or put it back.

maths.problem: Plot a line graph for the fine soil in the Water Climb test: 1 centimetre at 15 minutes, 2 at 30, 4 at 60. Then plot the sand: 6 at 15, 9 at 30, then the top (10) at 60. Which line is steeper at the start? What does this say about speed?
maths.answer: The sand line. Sand climbs faster at the start.
maths.explain: The sand rises 6 centimetres in the first 15 minutes, and the fine soil only 1. A steeper line means faster. Both lines flatten later because the water slows as it climbs.
maths.why_maths: A line graph shows speed as steepness, so you can compare two climbs at a glance.
maths.context: This is about the made-up results for the Water Climb test.

maths.problem: Saucer D in the Salty Seeds test had 1 teaspoon of salt, about 6 grams, in 100 millilitres of water. How many grams would that be in 1 litre? Sea water has about 35 grams of salt in a litre. How many times saltier than the sea was saucer D?
maths.answer: 60 grams in a litre. About 1.7 times saltier than the sea.
maths.explain: 1 litre is 10 lots of 100 millilitres, so 10 times 6 is 60 grams. 60 divided by 35 is about 1.7. So saucer D was nearly twice as salty as the sea.
maths.why_maths: Scaling up from a small saucer to a litre lets you compare the test with real sea water.
maths.context: This is about the Salty Seeds test, where seeds sat in water with different amounts of salt.

maths.problem: In the plain saucer, 9 of 10 seeds sprouted. In the saucer with half a teaspoon of salt, 2 of 10 sprouted. How many fewer seeds sprouted in the salty saucer? Out of every 10, what fraction less?
maths.answer: 7 fewer seeds. 7 out of 9, or about three quarters, fewer.
maths.explain: 9 take away 2 is 7. 7 out of the 9 that sprouted in plain water is a bit more than three quarters. So salt cut sprouting by about three quarters.
maths.why_maths: A fraction says how big the loss is compared with the plain saucer, which a plain subtraction does not.
maths.context: This is about the made-up results of the Salty Seeds test.

maths.problem: In the Cover or Bare test, the pale dry layer in the bare cup grew 6 millimetres each day. How thick was it after 5 days if it kept growing at that speed? Why might it not?
maths.answer: 30 millimetres, but in real life it may grow more slowly.
maths.explain: 6 times 5 is 30. But once the top layer is dry, water has further to climb to reach the surface, so the drying slows down.
maths.why_maths: Extending a number pattern is a quick way to predict, and it is also a way to ask where the pattern may break.
maths.context: This is about the Cover or Bare test, where the top of bare soil dried to a pale layer.

maths.problem: A farm follows this pattern: rice, black gram, ragi, rice, black gram, ragi, and so on. What will be grown in the 11th season? Explain how you worked it out.
maths.explain: The pattern repeats every 3 seasons. 11 divided by 3 is 3 with 2 left over. The second crop in the pattern is black gram.
maths.why_maths: Finding a place in a repeating pattern lets a farmer plan far ahead.
maths.context: This is about a crop rotation that repeats every three seasons.

maths.problem: A classroom holds 200 cubic metres of air. About 78 of every 100 parts of air are nitrogen. About how many cubic metres of nitrogen are in the room?
maths.explain: 78 out of 100 is 78 per cent. Half of 200 is 100, and 78 per cent of 200 is 2 times 78, which is 156. So most of the air in the room is nitrogen, and plants cannot use it.
maths.why_maths: Percentages show how large a share of a space a gas fills.
maths.context: This is about how much of the air around us is nitrogen.

maths.problem: A groundnut plant has 36 nodules, and each is about 3 millimetres across. If you laid them in a row, how long would the row be in centimetres?
maths.explain: 36 times 3 is 108 millimetres. 10 millimetres make 1 centimetre, so 108 millimetres is 10.8 centimetres.
maths.why_maths: Changing millimetres to centimetres lets you picture how big all the nodules are together.
maths.context: This is about the nodules on a groundnut plant's roots.

maths.problem: Fertiliser A costs 600 rupees for a 45 kilogram bag of urea with 46 per cent nitrogen. Fertiliser B costs 1,200 rupees for a 50 kilogram bag of a mix with 19 per cent nitrogen. Which gives more nitrogen for the money?
maths.answer: A gives more. About 20.7 kilograms for 600 rupees against 9.5 kilograms for 1,200 rupees.
maths.explain: 46 per cent of 45 is about 20.7 kilograms. 19 per cent of 50 is 9.5 kilograms. A gives about twice as much nitrogen for half the money. B also has other nutrients, so it is not a simple comparison.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the amount of nitrogen for the money shows that the cheapest bag is not always the best buy, and the bag labels matter.
maths.context: This is about the prices of two fertiliser bags. The prices are made up.

how_we_found_out.story: More than two thousand years ago, Roman farm writers told farmers to grow lupins and beans to enrich a field, but nobody knew why. In the 1800s many chemists believed that plants take all their nitrogen from the soil, and that beans were no different. Careful field trials at Rothamsted in England seemed to agree. Then in the 1880s two German scientists, Hermann Hellriegel and Hermann Wilfarth, grew peas and cereals in pots of pure sand with no nitrogen. The cereals starved. Peas starved too, unless the sand was watered with a little water from garden soil. Then the peas grew well and had nodules on their roots. When the soil water was heated first, the peas starved again. Something alive in the soil water was helping. In 1888 Martinus Beijerinck grew the bacteria from the nodules.
how_we_found_out.who: Hermann Hellriegel and Hermann Wilfarth, German scientists, and Martinus Beijerinck, a Dutch scientist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many chemists believed that plants take all their nitrogen from the soil, and that no plant could use nitrogen from the air. Hellriegel and Wilfarth showed that peas could grow on nitrogen from the air, but only when helped by living things in the soil.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. Water Climb needs dry materials, so dry the sand and gravel in the Sun for a day first, and rub the soil through a tea strainer. Sand is often wet to the top of an 11 centimetre cup within an hour, gravel climbs only about a centimetre, and fine soil is slow to start and may need until the next morning. Dry potting mix with a lot of cocopeat may resist water at first. A grown-up makes the holes in the cups. Salty Seeds uses very small amounts of salt in 100 millilitres, because moong is sensitive: the plain saucer should sprout in about two days, the pinch saucer a little slower, and the half spoon and spoon saucers few or none. If all four sprout alike, try fresh seeds. Cover or Bare needs a sunny window and clear cups. A rainy week will slow the drying, so use a warm dry spell. Nodules only form if the right bacteria are in the soil, so Bean Before Methi uses garden soil where beans have grown, and the step says what to do if no nodules are found. The Soil Bank game was checked on paper for eight seasons: rice every season fails from season 2, while rice alternating with a pulse keeps the bank above zero. Facts to verify: the 2003 soybean sanction study, the Oaxaca maize report, the Haber-Bosch share of world food, and the reach of capillary rise in different soils.
